shifts.claim: A 'proved' count can rise for the wrong reason: models learn to write weak or trivial specs that the prover accepts.
shifts.because: Re:Form reports that verification-only rewards led to trivial specification clauses and needed a subset reward (GTpre=>GENpre, GTpre=>(GENpost=>GTpost)). dawnr's published count needs a spec-strength column before any RL or self-play round.

shifts.claim: Executable specs can leak the implementation, and then the proof is trivial.
shifts.because: CLEVER found that with computable specs GPT-4o copied the spec into the implementation and proved it by rewriting, so it switched to non-computable specs. dawnr should measure how often t programs restate their spec.

shifts.claim: Data may not be the hard limit: a 3B model generated its own verified training problems.
shifts.because: PSV used no human data, only verifier-filtered self-proposed Verus specs, and raised pass@1 2.6-5.7x. The levers were solution verification, difficulty-aware proposing and proposal diversity, not more human rows.

shifts.claim: Retrieval of similar proved rows may beat a bigger model on CPU.
shifts.because: In Rango, adding similar proofs to a 1.3B model's context proved 47% more theorems, while lemma retrieval added only 3%.

shifts.claim: End-to-end verified code generation is hard for every model, including frontier ones, so a high refusal rate is the expected state of the field and not unique to a 4B model.
shifts.because: VERINA: the best model (o3) got 4.9% proof success in one trial with 52.3% of specs sound and complete. CLEVER: 1 of 161 problems verified end to end by any approach.

shifts.claim: Deterministic, model-free repair (pruning, mutation, hints) is a cheap source of extra proved answers that dawnr may be under-using.
shifts.because: SpecGen's mutation phase added 61 of 279 verified programs, and DafnyPro's 8 fixed hint strategies were its largest single gain (~10%) alongside pruning of non-inductive invariant clauses.

shifts.claim: Verifying people's ordinary Python directly through staged formalization is a credible alternative audience path to asking them to use t.
shifts.because: NFV formalises Python into Dafny/CBMC obligations in stages and reaches 92% precision, against 72% for an LLM judge and 50% for an unstaged agent.

areas.not_found: Not found or not fetchable: code or licence for AutoSpec/AutoSpec+ (ACSL spec synthesis) and SpecGen's artifact; any DafnyPro code; a licence file for PSV (abwilf/psv shows none); the CoqStoq data licence; the method details of VeriEquivBench's equivalence score (the abstract does not give them); the Lemur and NeuralInvariantRanker repos (not fetched); a permissively licensed Why3 or ACSL verified-code corpus; Dafny<->Verus/Lean translators with a released tool; a Kimina-Prover small-model card (not fetched, left out). Kani (MIT/Apache, Rust contracts) and Nagini (MPL-2.0, Python verifier) were fetched but left out as lower fit (Rust audience; MPL not on the licence list).

shifts.claim: RL on the 4B student will mostly raise pass@1, not the set of problems it can ever solve. Coverage comes from distillation and from searching with the prover.
shifts.because: Across model families, base models beat their RLVR versions at large k. On LiveCodeBench, Qwen2.5-7B scores 50% pass@128 vs 42.8% for Code-R1. Distilled models sit above the base at every k.

shifts.claim: A verifier reward on specs is not enough: on its own it trains vacuous specs. dawnr's 'complete specification' bottleneck needs a reward checked by a prover for dominance or completeness, and the wrong 'LLM reward' label on Re:Form in t/RELATED-WORK.md should be fixed.
shifts.because: Re:Form saw the model omit clauses until it added a subset reward, which Dafny checks, requiring the generated spec to imply the reference spec.

shifts.claim: 'Holding output to the grammar gained nothing' is expected. Constrain only the program region after free reasoning.
shifts.because: CRANE proves restrictive grammars reduce reasoning; constrained decoding fell below unconstrained for Qwen2.5-1.5B (22% vs 26%), while switching modes reached 31%.

shifts.claim: Whole-program self-repair with error text is not worth its compute at small size. Repair pays when the checker localises the failing subgoal and only that part is resampled.
shifts.because: Olausson et al. found self-repair gains at matched cost are 'modest ... sometimes not present', limited by feedback quality. Meanwhile APOLLO's compiler-localised hole repair cut samples from 25,600 to about 362 at higher accuracy, and Verina found Lean-feedback refinement 'reliably outperforms direct generation at matched query budgets'.

shifts.claim: Any dawnr RL gain on a Qwen base needs a random-reward control and a second model family before it is reported.
shifts.because: GRPO with random rewards raised Qwen2.5-Math-7B on MATH-500 by 21.4 pts vs 29.1 with true rewards; the effect did not appear on Llama3 or OLMo2.

shifts.claim: Small models fine-tuned on in-domain verified data can match frontier models on formal-verification tasks; the 4B bet is limited by data and search, not size.
shifts.because: A LoRA-fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B reaches 68% on DafnyBench with DafnyPro, Re:Form's 0.5B SFT model writes verifiable Dafny, and PSV at 3B improved pass@1 2.6x to 9.6x over expert iteration.

shifts.claim: Expect self-play to help a 4B model less than a 14B one; seed it with distilled or teacher data and do not rely on self-play alone.
shifts.because: Absolute Zero's gain grows with base size (3B +5.7, 7B +10.2, 14B +13.2), and smaller models plateau sooner.

areas.not_found: I could not fetch a licence or location for the F* PoPAI dataset (fstar-lang.org/popai returns 404, and no FStarLang/PoPAI repo exists). I found no repo for dafny-annotator or a licence for DafnySynth, and could not tell which model generated DafnySynth. The PSV and Pass@k Training repos have no licence file. Verina's licence conflicts: the HF tag says Apache-2.0, but the paper says GPL-3.0 from MBPP-DFY-50. I found no published negative result for type-constrained or semantic decoding on Dafny or Verus, and no open preference-tuning (DPO) work that uses formal-verifier outcomes at 1B to 10B. Left out because dawnr's docs already cover them: Lahiri spec symbolic testing (nl-2-postcond, already in t/spec_quality.py), Verina, Large Language Monkeys, STP, and 1-shot RLVR. LeDex was left out of findings because it is CC BY-NC-ND and its data was generated by GPT-3.5.

shifts.claim: For extraction, the 4B generative step may be unnecessary. A 0.2B span reader returns offsets inside the source by construction, so the 4B model's role shrinks to choosing fields, or it drops out.
shifts.because: deberta-v3-base-squad2 reports 83.8 EM on SQuAD 2.0 dev. dawnr's grammar-held 4B extractor got 165/300 answerable exact because it copied whole sentences. The numbers are not on the same split, but the gap points to an architecture problem.

shifts.claim: For a scan, a verbatim quote certifies the OCR transcript, not the page. OCR and VLM parsers are models that write the 'source', so a scan needs two independent readers that agree, or the page crop shown beside the quote.
shifts.because: The best small parsers (PaddleOCR-VL 0.9B, GLM-OCR 0.9B, granite-docling) are generative VLMs. Their own scores are below perfect, for example full-page OCR F1 0.84 for granite-docling.

shifts.claim: The cite bottleneck is finding the right sentence, not quoting it verbatim. Effort belongs in ranking sentences and retrieval, not in more decoding constraints.
shifts.because: FullCite with Qwen3-8B and constrained decoding over a citation grammar: document-level F1 33.87 but snippet-level F1 12.80. Over 80% of BioASQ citations went to the first two documents.

shifts.claim: Report 'correct and attributable' as the headline document metric. Accuracy against a gold answer overstates what can be trusted, which supports dawnr's quote-or-refuse design.
shifts.because: In XOR-AttriQA, up to 50% of answers that exactly matched the gold reference were not attributable to the retrieved passage.

shifts.claim: Fine-tuning on domain documents can raise numeric fabrication sharply. Every dawnr fine-tune for document or number tasks should be checked with a 'numbers not in the source' rule before and after.
shifts.because: A finance fine-tune went from a 5.4% hallucination rate in the base model to 82.5% overt numeric hallucination, and 98% after further stages.

shifts.claim: rag_cite gates support with AlignScore, which is a model, contrary to 'a language model is never the check'. The extract design (the value must be a span of the quoted sentence) is the non-model version, and cite could adopt it: the answer must be a substring of its quote.
shifts.because: The attribution literature finds NLI models and fine-tuned LLMs are the best detectors, which places such support gates on the model side of dawnr's line.

shifts.claim: Contract and finance reviewers are an audience dawnr has not targeted, for whom 'quote the clause or say it is not there' is already the norm. Expert, permissively licensed benchmarks for them exist.
shifts.because: CUAD has 13k+ expert labels on 510 contract PDFs (CC-BY-4.0). ContractNLI has 607 NDAs with evidence spans and a 'NotMentioned' label (CC-BY-4.0).

areas.not_found: I found no rule-based (non-model) entailment checker that is alive and permissively licensed. The numeric-hallucination work uses only regex or arithmetic checks, and no tool was released with it. RecaLLM's verbatim-recall decoding has Apache-2.0 code, but its SFT data was written by GPT-5.2 and its bases are Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B, so it is an idea only. The FullCite code and licence were not on the page. Marker's code is Apache-2.0, but its weights are under a modified OpenRAIL-M licence with a $5M revenue limit, so I excluded it. MinerU's licence shows NOASSERTION, so I excluded it. I did not fetch a CPU throughput number for PaddleOCR-VL or for the CUAD baselines. No attributed-QA benchmark built from personal documents (email, receipts, letters) under a permissive licence turned up.

shifts.claim: Gold, human-written rules turn the spec bottleneck into a fact-parsing task. For everyday domains, dawnr should ship hand-written spec and rule libraries (Catala law, calculators, constraint templates) and have the 4B model fill in only the facts, rather than writing the program and the spec.
shifts.because: With gold Prolog statutes, GPT-5 few-shot got 86 of 100 SARA cases; the paper credits the gold statutes with reducing reliance on the model's parsing of the law. dawnr's own record says writing a right, complete spec is the bottleneck.

shifts.claim: The answer rate should be scored with prices, not as a raw count of 17/182: price each refusal at the cost of the human alternative and each wrong answer at its penalty, then report a break-even cost.
shifts.because: The tax paper prices abstention at $270 and errors at IRS penalties; its best system breaks even at $15.78 per return. Under that scoring, a gate that refuses often can still be shown to be worth using.

shifts.claim: Where no prover or spec exists (tax, SQL, constraints), two independent formalizations that agree can be the check, which extends dawnr's principle beyond the seven provers.
shifts.because: The winning tax configuration required two independent solver-backed solutions to agree before answering; QED can prove two SQL queries equivalent (about 290 of about 440 Calcite cases).

shifts.claim: A deterministic data-flow gate on tool calls costs little utility. dawnr's 'arguments were said' rule is a narrow case of capability and information-flow tracking and could become the full design (plan from the trusted query only, label every value).
shifts.because: CaMeL solves 77% of AgentDojo tasks with provable security against 84% undefended, a 7-point cost; FIDES enforces integrity and confidentiality labels deterministically.

shifts.claim: Checker-only reward is enough to train a small model well; dawnr can train with prover acceptance as the whole reward.
shifts.because: Arctic-Text2SQL-R1-7B used only execution correctness and syntax validity as GRPO rewards and reached 68.5% on BIRD-test.

shifts.claim: There is an everyday audience where checked computation beats frontier models outright: tax and fee calculations, where the strongest models still fail a third of returns.
shifts.because: On TaxCalcBench v2 (tax year 2025) the best model reaches 66% strict accuracy, while the expected outputs come from a deterministic tax engine. This is the gap a fact-extraction-plus-rules engine is built for.

shifts.claim: Declarative constraint models may be easier for models to write correctly than verified imperative programs, so a constraint fragment checked by a solver could lift the answer rate on planning-type questions.
shifts.because: On DCP-Bench-Open, CPMpy modelling reached about 70% at baseline and 90.2% with inference-time methods, with solution-level checking.

areas.not_found: I looked for an Apache or MIT rules-as-code engine for US benefits; PolicyEngine-US is AGPL-3.0, so it is idea only. I looked for a code repository for Progent: the arXiv page links none, and its policies are model-generated and checked deterministically with an SMT solver for expansion. I looked for a permissively licensed statistics-applicability benchmark: StatQA is GPL-3.0. I looked for the per-row generator in SynSQL-2.5M: the HF card returned 401, and the paper lists Llama 3.1 among the generators, so the data is not usable for training without filtering. I did not find an open dosage or drug-label rules engine. Fetched but cut for space: Test of Time (CC-BY-4.0, 2,800 date-arithmetic rows, training explicitly prohibited, so evaluation only); Logic-LM (MIT, Z3/Prover9/Pyke, +39.2% over the plain LLM); Invariant Guardrails (Apache-2.0, deterministic flow rules over agent traces); Pint (BSD units library); Duckling (BSD, Haskell, 13 dimensions); ARM causality-laundering monitor (no code released).

shifts.claim: A speech recognizer is itself a language model writing text, so dawnr's rule that a language model is never the check covers whisper.cpp. A transcript is not evidence until something acoustic (CTC alignment score, VAD span, word confidence) agrees with it.
shifts.because: About 1% of Whisper transcriptions contained whole invented phrases or sentences. 38% of those were harmful, and the rate was higher for speakers with long pauses.

shifts.claim: Checking a given text against audio is far easier than writing it, which is the asymmetry dawnr relies on for programs. Quotes from recordings should be checked by aligning the proposed text, not by trusting a second ASR.
shifts.because: NFA with the true text reached 98.35% precision. With ASR-predicted text it fell to 85.65% precision and 71.09% recall, and WhisperX to 90.26% and 70.12%.

shifts.claim: For reading documents, a tiny specialist trained with RL beats a huge generalist. dawnr should add vision as separate small specialists behind checks, not move to one large multimodal model.
shifts.because: OvisOCR2 (0.8B, on Qwen3.5-0.8B) and TeleOCR (1.2B) lead OmniDocBench at about 96.6-96.9. Qwen3-VL-235B scores 89.78.

shifts.claim: dawnr's deterministic checks can be training rewards for the document reader, not only gates. The binding limit is a permissive generator of synthetic test documents, since AI2's was Claude.
shifts.because: Binary unit-test rewards with GRPO took olmOCR from 78.5 to 82.4. The synthetic HTML and tests came from Claude Sonnet 4.

shifts.claim: An Apache or MIT tag on the weights does not clear a model for dawnr. The licence gate has to read each card's training-data section too.
shifts.because: Molmo2-4B is Apache-2.0 but trained on datasets restricted to academic, non-commercial research use. Kokoro-82M (Apache-2.0) used synthetic audio from closed commercial TTS. openWakeWord's models are CC-BY-NC-SA because of their training data.

shifts.claim: Do not build speech alignment on torchaudio. It has been removed.
shifts.because: torchaudio entered maintenance in 2.9: the forced-alignment APIs were deprecated in 2.8 and removed in 2.9, and its MMS_FA bundle is Meta's MMS model.

areas.not_found: These were left out because a fetched page did not settle them: a licence for the sherpa-onnx gigaspeech KWS model (none stated), word confidence in NeMo-Speech.cpp (not documented), NFA's own licence line, the CPU speed of Kokoro, and benchmark numbers for Qwen3-VL-2B (the card gave none). Fetched but not listed: Vosk (Apache-2.0 but older), Moondream2 (Apache-2.0, 2B), RF-DETR (closed-vocabulary detection, so not a check on claims), Montreal Forced Aligner (MIT; English model CC-BY-4.0; NFA beats it). KittenTTS weights were excluded because they carry per-model and community licences. The NFA paper PDF was read with pdftotext after WebFetch failed on it.

shifts.claim: Split dawnr by where each check can run. The quote, extract, arithmetic and tool-argument checks are plain code that can run in a browser tab or on a phone; only the provers need a real machine. Ship the light checks everywhere first rather than waiting until every prover can be installed.
shifts.because: Browser llama.cpp (wllama) and phone llama.cpp (PocketPal) are released and current. The provers do not travel: Z3 does reach the browser via npm, but Rocq-in-browser (jsCoq) is AGPL and stuck at Coq 8.17-8.21, and Dafny has no shown browser path.

shifts.claim: The model is becoming something the operating system or browser provides. dawnr's lasting value is the checker and the replayable certificate, which could sit in front of any local model, including one the user already has.
shifts.because: Chrome 138+ ships a built-in on-device model (Gemini Nano) with a JSON-schema responseConstraint to web pages. It needs 22 GB of disk and 16 GB RAM or a GPU with more than 4 GB, so a model is arriving on desktops without anyone installing one. (Its outputs could only be checked, never used as training data.)

shifts.claim: On a CPU, the answer rate may be set by how many prove-and-repair attempts fit in the user's patience, not only by model quality. Decoding speed is an answer-rate lever.
shifts.because: SuffixDecoding reports up to 5.3x speedups precisely on self-refinement and agentic loops with repeated text, which is the shape of dawnr's repair loop. DFlash ships a drafter for Qwen3.5-4B.

shifts.claim: Comparable open projects gained users mostly as a backend other apps plug into, or with a one-command install, not through their own UI alone. dawnr should be selectable inside apps people already run.
shifts.because: Ollama's onboarding is one curl/PowerShell line, an OpenAI-compatible API and a long list of third-party integrations. AnythingLLM and Jan both consume such OpenAI/Ollama-style providers.

shifts.claim: A browser-only zero-install path would miss Linux, dawnr's main platform today, so a native installer stays necessary.
shifts.because: WebGPU shipped in Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari by Nov 2025, but Linux support is still 'in progress' across all browsers. Firefox covers only Windows and macOS ARM64.

shifts.claim: An unconsidered audience is offline hotspots: one box runs the model and provers, and nearby phones use dawnr's page over local Wi-Fi. That matches the 'spaceship' framing better than one laptop per person.
shifts.because: Internet-in-a-Box serves schools, clinics and prisons from a Raspberry Pi and serves nearby phones and tablets; it currently bundles no local AI. Its code is GPL-2.0, so this is idea-only: dawnr would be an add-on app, not copied code.

shifts.claim: A dense 4B may not be the fastest shape for CPU users. Sparse or hybrid models with about 1B active parameters per token should be on the base-model ladder.
shifts.because: Granite-4.0-H-Tiny (Apache-2.0) has 7B total and 1B active parameters, scoring HumanEval 83 and MBPP 80.

areas.not_found: Release dates or numbers for Dafny running in a browser via .NET WebAssembly: the search hinted at net*-browser targets but nothing fetched confirms it. CPU (not GPU) speedup figures for DFlash or SuffixDecoding. Moonshine's WER and latency table: the models doc page did not render it. Specifics of Apple's Foundation Models framework: the page is script-rendered and the fetch came back generic, so it was left out. Real download or user counts for Jan, Ollama, PocketPal or AnythingLLM: their READMEs give only stars. Training code for the DFlash drafters, needed if dawnr fine-tunes the 4B.

shifts.claim: Refusals are partly a routing problem, not only a model-quality problem: a 4B model already knows, before writing, whether its code will be right.
shifts.because: A linear probe on Qwen3-4B's final prompt state predicts first-attempt correctness at AUC 0.881. dawnr can put CPU time on the problems likely to be proved and refuse the others quickly, before chasing a bigger model.

shifts.claim: 'Up to seven provers agree' is less independent than it sounds; Dafny's result rests on Boogie plus an SMT solver such as Z3, and soundness bugs have been found in both Dafny's verifier and compiler.
shifts.because: Independence should be counted by trusted base (Z3-backed vs kernel-checked vs proof-certificate-checked), and the certificate should carry checkable proof objects where possible (Carcara for Alethe, nanoda for Lean, coqchk for Rocq).

shifts.claim: dawnr is a small working instance of 'Guaranteed Safe AI' (world model + safety specification + verifier that emits an auditable proof certificate). That framing comes with an audience of researchers and safety funders who have few running examples.
shifts.because: Bengio, Russell, Tegmark, Dalrymple and others propose exactly this three-part architecture for safety-critical AI. dawnr's certificate and spec bottleneck map onto it, which gives a vocabulary and a community beyond 'local assistant'.

shifts.claim: Refusal need not be all-or-nothing for unprovable answers: back off to a less specific answer that still meets a calibrated correctness level.
shifts.because: Conformal factuality reaches 80-90% correctness guarantees while keeping most of the output. For documents, dawnr could release the subset of quoted sentences that clears a calibrated threshold instead of refusing outright.

shifts.claim: Do not lean on the model's own refusals for unanswerable or underspecified questions; reasoning training makes them worse.
shifts.because: Reasoning fine-tuning degrades abstention by 24% on average across 20 datasets. If dawnr trains a reasoning student, the external gate must carry all abstention, and 'unanswerable' document questions need their own non-model check.

shifts.claim: Prover order matters for the answer rate: on the same problems a strong model does about five times better in Dafny than in Lean.
shifts.because: AlgoVeri reports 40.3% Dafny vs 24.7% Verus vs 7.8% Lean, and says Verus and Lean trap models in syntax and semantics. t should try the most forgiving target first and report per-prover rates.

shifts.claim: Spec completeness can be scored by a number, not only read by hand: count how many defective (mutant) implementations the spec rejects while it still accepts correct runs.
shifts.because: POSTCONDBENCH (420 tasks) uses defect discrimination as completeness and finds a large correctness-completeness gap in five frontier LLMs. A fine-tuned 7B matched GPT-4o on postconditions in the companion study, which supports a small spec writer behind dawnr's gate.

areas.not_found: Not found: a permissive SAE suite for Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen-Scope is under the Qwen licence and the pages I fetched showed no 4B checkpoint). The Sigsum project pages would not load, so its licence is unconfirmed beyond a search snippet and Sigsum is left out of the findings. A per-answer signing scheme designed for LLM outputs (rather than files or media) did not turn up. Neither did deterministic or batch-invariant inference for llama.cpp on CPU; only SGLang documents it, on GPU. For verifier-based abstention on code, 'When to Answer and When to Defer' (arXiv 2605.19369) had no code release, so it is left out. A licence for the AbstentionBench repo is not stated (GitHub reports NOASSERTION), so it appears only as a shift. The CycloneDX ML-BOM page gave no spec version or signing details. PyPI dates for model-signing would not load; release dates come from the GitHub API.

shifts.claim: Treat the answer rate first as a sampling and search budget problem, and only then as a training problem. Measure coverage@k before the next training round.
shifts.because: With an automatic verifier, coverage converts directly into solved problems and rises log-linearly with samples (15.9% to 56% at 250 samples), while unverified selection plateaus. dawnr already has the verifier, so it may be leaving most of its answer rate unsampled.

shifts.claim: dawnr's most durable product may be the checker toolkit (t, the gate, replayable certificates) that any model can use, more than its own 4B model.
shifts.because: ARIA's GBP 59M Safeguarded AI programme stopped funding specialised AI teams because frontier models beat expectations ('more likely than not we'd select zero successful teams for Phase 2'). It now funds the TA1 tooling for mathematical assurance and auditability.

shifts.claim: The specification should be agreed with the person through examples they approve, not written completely by the model. A refusal over a weak spec should become a question.
shifts.because: Test-driven intent formalization added about 46 points of pass@1 within 5 interactions, and users judged code correctness better with less cognitive load. Separately, LLM-written postconditions caught 64 real bugs, so specs are checkable artefacts in their own right.

shifts.claim: Replace answer-or-refuse with graded, exact verdicts: proved, proved under named assumptions, partially proved (the strongest sub-spec), and ambiguous (several readings).
shifts.because: AWS's shipped checker reports valid, invalid, satisfiable (depends on assumptions) and ambiguous. Conformal back-off keeps most of the output while guaranteeing what is kept. Both turn would-be refusals into honest, narrower answers.

shifts.claim: Frame 'trustworthy for a spaceship' as a guarantee about symbolic answers relative to a stated spec. Certificates should name that spec, and the trusted checker deserves its own verification.
shifts.because: Dickson argues proofs hold only for symbol systems, not physical outcomes. GSAI's own reply concedes guarantees are 'relative to' simplified models and keeps them useful only if those models are sound. The GSAI framework names three parts (world model, safety spec, verifier); dawnr makes the third explicit, but the first two are mostly implicit.

shifts.claim: Repair loops should feed only sound checker output (prover errors, counterexamples) back to the model. Self-critique steps should be removed rather than tuned.
shifts.because: With GPT-4 on Game of 24, graph colouring and STRIPS planning, self-critique collapsed performance while a sound external verifier gave significant gains, and much of the critique machinery could be removed without loss. LLM-Modulo planning gained 4.6x from external critics.

shifts.claim: The 4B may be doing too much. Have it propose small creative pieces (an invariant, a lemma, a spec clause) and let deterministic search build the rest.
shifts.because: In AlphaGeometry a 152M model that only proposes auxiliary constructions lifts a symbolic engine from 14/30 to 25/30 IMO problems. The division of labour mattered more than model size.

shifts.claim: Expect fine-tuning gains to show up in-distribution and fade on the held-out panel. A small domain model can still beat a much larger general one in its own domain.
shifts.because: Li and Ellis found fine-tuned LLMs are strong at programming by example only when test problems are in-distribution. FLAME (60M, Excel-specific tokenizer) beat 175B Codex in 10 of 14 settings. The clean 182 is exactly the out-of-distribution test that exposes this.

shifts.claim: There is a ready audience dawnr has not targeted: rules as code for law, benefits and tax, where governments and legal-aid groups already want answers with explanations a lawyer can review.
shifts.because: Catala (Inria, Apache-2.0) produces lawyer-readable output so domain experts can certify code against law articles. Blawx (MIT) gives non-programmers explained answers over encoded rules. Both lack the natural-language front end dawnr has.

areas.not_found: Catala production users: catala-lang.org returned only its title, so I list no government uses. FinQA: the README does not give the dataset size. Query4Regex: the README does not say who wrote the natural-language forms (a person or a model). VeriEQL: I did not check the artifact licence on Zenodo. The Dafny spec-hacking result (RLVR 9.7% to 31.1% after filtering weak specs) appeared only in a search snippet; the paper I fetched (AxDafny, arXiv 2606.32007) did not show those numbers, so I left it out. Certora Prover is GPL-3.0 and its README says nothing about how specs are written, so I left it out. lean4game is GPL-3.0 (left out). I found no permissively licensed hardware-assertion (SystemVerilog) project, no medicine or finance checker with a licence dawnr could train on (MedCalc-Bench is CC-BY-SA), and no user study measuring how people react to a high refusal rate.

findings.name: Re:Form subset reward (Veri-Code/ReForm)
findings.licence: MIT (repo README); Python2Dafny data written by Claude 3.5 Sonnet per paper arXiv 2507.16331
findings.what: RL for Dafny code+spec generation with small Qwen models (0.5B-14B) and a reward that checks a generated spec is at least as strong as a reference spec.
findings.steal: Add a 'spec strength' gate to dawnr's spec check: prove GTpre => GENpre and GTpre => (GENpost => GTpost) against a reference spec with the existing provers, and use the same check as the reward for any t RL round.
findings.moves: Answer rate and trust: stops weak or vacuous specs counting as proved; gives a verifier-based reward for spec writing, the named bottleneck
findings.evidence: Paper: verification-only rewards produced trivial specs; with the subset reward the 14B RL model reaches 14.0% pass@1 on DafnyComp vs 8.3% SFT-only; 0.5B SFT passes over 80% validation
findings.risk: Data and the released weights come from Claude 3.5 Sonnet translations, so neither can be dawnr training data; take only the reward formula and code.

findings.name: Propose, Solve, Verify (PSV)
findings.licence: code at github.com/abwilf/psv: no licence file visible; paper CC BY 4.0
findings.what: Self-play for verified code: a proposer writes Verus specs, a solver is trained by expert iteration, and the verifier is the only signal; no human data, base Qwen2.5-Coder-3B.
findings.steal: Run a PSV loop on t: the dawnr model proposes new t specs, filtered by the spec checker and difficulty (solve rate), and the solver trains on rows the provers accept. This becomes a self-generating source of rows in the training pipeline.
findings.moves: Data scarcity (a few thousand accepted rows) and answer rate
findings.evidence: 3B model pass@1: Dafny2Verus 24.06%->65.63%, MBPP 6.48%->36.78%, HumanEval 7.24%->19.07%; ablations: no solution verification -51.5%, no difficulty-aware proposing -5.6%, fixed prompts -10.6%; only 47.7% of proposed specs valid
findings.risk: No licence on the repo, so reimplement from the paper and do not copy code; proposed specs need dawnr's held-out contamination audit.

findings.name: Rango (proof + premise retrieval)
findings.licence: MIT (repo); paper arXiv 2412.14063; CoqStoq data licence not stated
findings.what: Rocq proof synthesis that retrieves similar already-proved proofs from the same project into the context of a fine-tuned 1.3B model at every step.
findings.steal: At inference, retrieve the k most similar proved t rows (program+spec+proof) from dawnr's accepted corpus into the 4B prompt. This is cheap on CPU and needs no retraining.
findings.moves: Answer rate on CPU without a bigger model
findings.evidence: Proof retriever gives +47% theorems proved vs the variant without it; lemma retriever only +3%; Rango proves 32.0% on CoqStoq benchmark (paper)
findings.risk: Rango's model is a DeepSeek-Coder fine-tune (not a permissive base), so take only the retrieval method; retrieved rows must exclude held-out panel neighbours.

findings.name: CrossHair
findings.licence: MIT for most sources, plus Apache-2.0 and PSF parts (LICENSE)
findings.what: SMT-backed symbolic execution of Python contracts, with test generation (cover) and behaviour diffing (diffbehavior) between two functions.
findings.steal: Use diffbehavior between dawnr's Python hand-back and the reference, and symbolic contract checks, as a cheap counterexample finder before spending prover time. It also extends the spec check beyond example-size inputs.
findings.moves: Spec check strength (larger-inputs gap) and Python breadth for ordinary users
findings.evidence: 2,401 commits on main; three modes: contracts, cover, diffbehavior; the docs state limits (it is not a proof)
findings.risk: Not sound or complete, so it can only be a refuter and never a passing check; it is slow on heavy library code.

findings.name: nl-2-postcond / intent-formalization (Microsoft)
findings.what: Artifacts for NL-to-postcondition studies: test-set correctness plus a bug-completeness score that counts how many mutant implementations a postcondition rejects. Also includes AutoCLRS F* specs and FMCAD'24 Dafny/Verus intent-formalization evaluations.
findings.steal: Add a mutant-kill completeness score to dawnr's spec check: mutate the reference t program, and count a spec as complete only if it rejects the mutants that change behaviour. Report it beside 'proved'.
findings.moves: Spec completeness, the named bottleneck; also gives a trust number per answer
findings.evidence: Repo bundles TiCoder (TSE'24), the FSE'24 nl2postcond study and the FMCAD'24 evaluation; 67 commits
findings.risk: Postconditions in the study were produced by GPT-family models, so eval only; the mutant method itself is free.

findings.name: VERINA
findings.what: Lean 4 benchmark that scores code, specification and proof generation separately and in combination, with reference code, specs, proofs and tests.
findings.steal: Lift VERINA tasks into t as an extra held-out panel that scores spec soundness and completeness separately from proof, using its test.json to grade specs.
findings.moves: Measurement of the spec bottleneck separately from proof; a wider held-out panel
findings.evidence: Abstract: o3 gets 72.6% code correct, 52.3% specs sound and complete, 4.9% proof success (one trial)
findings.risk: Run heldout_audit for overlap with MBPP/HumanEval-derived rows; lifting from Lean into t may need hand work.

findings.name: CLEVER
findings.what: 161 HumanEval-derived Lean 4 problems with non-computable ground-truth specs. A model must prove its spec equivalent to the hidden spec, then prove its implementation correct.
findings.steal: Use as an evaluation panel and copy its 'spec certification' step: dawnr proves a generated t spec equivalent to a reference spec, rather than only testing it.
findings.moves: Spec trust; exposes spec-leak shortcuts
findings.evidence: Only 1 of 161 problems verified end-to-end by any evaluated approach (problem 53, add two integers)
findings.risk: HumanEval-derived, so contamination against dawnr's training rows must be audited; Lean only.

findings.name: Verus-Bench and VeruSAGE-Bench (AutoVerus)
findings.what: AutoVerus proof agent (generate, refine with tips, repair from verifier errors) plus 150 algorithm tasks and 849 repository-level Verus tasks.
findings.steal: Lift the 150 Verus-Bench algorithm tasks into t rows or panel items, and port AutoVerus's error-class-specific repair prompts into dawnr's prover-feedback repair loop.
findings.moves: Data rows; repair from prover feedback
findings.evidence: Paper: AutoVerus proves over 90% of 150 tasks, over half in under 30 s or 3 LLM calls; repo 192 commits, leaderboard included
findings.risk: Generated proofs in /generated are LLM-written (GPT family) and are eval only; VeruSAGE tasks are systems code, far from t.

findings.name: DafnyPro
findings.what: Dafny proof-annotation pipeline with a diff checker (code unchanged once annotations are stripped), iterative pruning of non-inductive invariant clauses, and 8 problem-independent hint strategies.
findings.steal: Add a Houdini-style pruner that drops failing invariant clauses one by one and re-verifies, plus a diff check that the model never edits the program or spec, in dawnr's repair loop. Both run without a model.
findings.moves: Answer rate via deterministic repair; protection against spec tampering
findings.evidence: Hint augmentation gave the largest gain (~10% on DafnyBench); fine-tuned Qwen 7B 68%, 14B 70% verified
findings.risk: No code release, so reimplement; numbers are on DafnyBench (contamination-prone).

findings.name: SpecGen mutation phase
findings.licence: none stated for code (paper arXiv non-exclusive)
findings.what: When a model's spec fails to verify, apply predicate, logical, comparative and arithmetic mutation operators to it and keep verifiable mutants by heuristic selection (Java/JML, OpenJML).
findings.steal: After a failed proof, mutate the model's t spec or invariants (<= to <, add/drop conjunct, quantifier bounds) and re-run the provers before refusing; keep only mutants that pass dawnr's spec strength/completeness check.
findings.moves: Answer rate without more model calls
findings.evidence: Mutation lifts 218 to 279 of 385 programs verified (+61); expert rating 4.54 vs oracle 4.83
findings.risk: Mutation can weaken specs to pass, so it must be gated by the subset/mutant-kill checks above.

findings.name: FStarDataSet-V2
findings.what: Human-written verified F* definitions, lemmas and proofs extracted from FStar, HACL* and Steel, with dependency and typing metadata.
findings.steal: Mine the small pure-functional lemmas and specs as a source for lifting into t, or use them as F* prover regression tests. This needs a decision that CDLA-P-2.0 is acceptable first.
findings.moves: Data scarcity (human-written, not model-generated)
findings.evidence: 54.4k rows: 30.9k train, 1.96k validation, 21.5k test
findings.risk: CDLA-Permissive-2.0 is not on dawnr's licence list; most content is crypto/systems code far from everyday t problems.

findings.name: dafny-annotator + DafnySynth pipeline
findings.what: LLM-guided search that adds Dafny annotations until verification, plus an 'edit graph' synthesis pipeline (idea proposer, implementer, annotator, change proposer).
findings.steal: Reuse the edit-graph data generator with dawnr's own permissive teacher writing t, so that each verified edit becomes a new row.
findings.moves: Data scarcity
findings.evidence: Paper: LoRA fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B goes from 15.7% to 50.6% of DafnyBench methods annotated
findings.risk: The released DafnySynth used GPT-4o in some editors and the models are Llama-based, so no data or weights; take the code only.

findings.name: Kimina Lean Server
findings.what: REST server that runs pooled Lean 4 REPLs with import reuse and gc, for batch proof checking.
findings.steal: Put dawnr's Lean leg behind it during grading and data generation so that Lean imports are not reloaded per row.
findings.moves: Prover throughput on lab CPUs (cheaper grading, more rows per hour)
findings.evidence: Defaults to CPU count minus 1 REPLs, 8 GB per REPL; Lean v4.26.0 default; paper reports 1.5-2x speedup
findings.risk: Memory-heavy (8 GB per REPL), so cap the REPL count on the lab beside training.

findings.name: Goedel-Prover-V2-8B
findings.what: Lean 4 whole-proof prover on Qwen3-8B with two rounds of compiler-feedback self-correction.
findings.steal: Use as an optional Lean lemma closer, invoked only when the t-to-Lean obligation fails, at Q4 on the desktop or lab.
findings.moves: Proof leg of the answer rate for Lean obligations
findings.evidence: MiniF2F test 83.0% at pass@32; PutnamBench 57 at pass@32
findings.risk: Trained for competition math, not program obligations; 8B is slow on a consumer CPU and needs pass@k.

findings.name: ESBMC (Python frontend)
findings.licence: Apache-2.0 mainly; third-party parts per COPYING
findings.what: SMT bounded model checker with k-induction for C, C++, Rust and type-annotated Python (division by zero, index errors, overflow, user assertions).
findings.steal: Check a user's own typed Python directly for runtime errors and asserts, as a refusal-or-pass check in the extract/calc paths, alongside t.
findings.moves: Breadth: verify mainstream Python for non-t users
findings.evidence: Supports C, C++, CUDA, CHERI, Kotlin, Python, Rust, Solidity; strategies include incremental BMC and k-induction
findings.risk: Bounded unless k-induction succeeds; Python subset needs annotations; it is a large C++ dependency to ship.

findings.name: FVAPPS
findings.licence: MIT (dataset card); specs generated by Claude 3.5 Sonnet per paper arXiv 2502.05714
findings.what: APPS problems with unit tests generalised into Lean 4 theorems stated with sorry, in three quality tiers.
findings.steal: Evaluation only: the 1,083 guarded-and-plausible items as a large hard panel for dawnr's Lean leg.
findings.moves: Wider evaluation of hard problems
findings.evidence: 4,715 unguarded, 2,089 guarded, 1,083 guarded+plausible (property-based tested)
findings.risk: Claude-written, so never training data; APPS overlap with dawnr sources requires the contamination audit.

findings.name: Neuro-Formal Verification (NFV)
findings.licence: paper CC-BY-4.0; no code release found
findings.what: Agent that formalises a Python verification question into Dafny proof obligations in staged steps, with CBMC as a counterexample backend.
findings.steal: Pattern for a 'bring your own Python' mode: stage the formalization (translate, state spec, prove) and keep each stage's artifact in the certificate.
findings.moves: Breadth: mainstream language verification; certificate design
findings.evidence: Dafny: 57% correct resolution at 92% precision; CBMC: 63% bug detection at 90% precision; LLM-as-judge 72% precision; unstaged agent 50%
findings.risk: No code; precision numbers are on its own balanced dataset.

findings.name: VeriEquivBench
findings.what: Benchmark that grades Dafny code+spec by a formal equivalence score instead of matching a hand-written ground-truth spec.
findings.steal: Idea only: score t spec/code pairs for mutual consistency without reference specs, so new self-play rows can be graded.
findings.moves: Spec evaluation at scale without hand-written references
findings.evidence: 2,389 algorithmic problems; revised April 2026
findings.risk: Non-commercial licence, so the data can never be used; method details were not in the fetched abstract.

findings.name: APOLLO (sorrify plus subgoal repair)
findings.licence: MIT (GitHub licence field); paper CC BY 4.0
findings.what: A repair loop driven by the Lean compiler. It fixes syntax, replaces failing blocks with sorry, tries automatic tactics on each hole, and recursively asks the LLM only about the sub-lemmas still open. Then it reassembles the proof and re-checks it.
findings.steal: Build a 'hole-and-recurse' repair stage in dawnr's prover driver. When a t program's proof fails, cut the failing assertion or lemma out as a hole, run the prover's automation on it, and resample only that hole with local context, never the whole program. Start on the Lean and Dafny legs.
findings.moves: Answer rate at a CPU sample budget
findings.evidence: Kimina-Prover-Distill-7B went from 70.8% to 75.0% on miniF2F with samples cut to 307; Goedel-Prover-SFT's budget fell from 25,600 to about 362. 84.9% for under-8B models at budget 128.
findings.risk: The code targets Lean 4 and Mathlib tactics; the Dafny, Verus and F* legs need their own hole operators. Last push Nov 2025.

findings.name: CRANE (constrain only the answer region)
findings.licence: MIT (GitHub licence field); paper CC BY 4.0
findings.what: Decoding that reasons without constraint and switches to grammar-constrained generation only between delimiters such as << >>. The paper also proves why a strict output grammar reduces reasoning.
findings.steal: Replace whole-output grammar holding in dawnr's t generation with CRANE switching: free reasoning first, then the t program between delimiters under the t grammar. This is a llama.cpp-side change to the existing GBNF use.
findings.moves: Answer rate; explains why the grammar gained nothing
findings.evidence: GSM-Symbolic, Qwen2.5-1.5B: 26% unconstrained, 22% constrained, 31% CRANE. FOLIO, Llama-3.1-8B: 32.0% to 46.3%.
findings.risk: The gains were measured on symbolic math and logic, not program synthesis. It adds reasoning tokens, which cost CPU time.

findings.name: Pass@k Training
findings.licence: none stated (repo RUCAIBox/Passk_Training has no licence)
findings.what: RLVR whose reward is pass@k over groups, with a closed-form advantage. It counters the conservative collapse of pass@1 GRPO.
findings.steal: Use the analytical pass@k advantage in dawnr's GRPO and expert-iteration weighting, since dawnr serves with sampling plus prover selection: train pass@k first, then pass@1.
findings.moves: Answer rate under sampling with a verifier
findings.evidence: Qwen2.5-7B on Enigmata: pass@1 training scored 12.9 pass@1 and 21.3 pass@8; pass@k training 17.9 and 29.8; both in sequence 30.8 and 40.6.
findings.risk: The repo has no licence, so reimplement from the paper's formula. Not tested on formal code.

findings.name: Goedel-Prover-V2 (scaffolded data, extract_goal, model averaging)
findings.licence: Apache-2.0 (HF model card tag for Goedel-Prover-V2-8B); GitHub repo has no licence file
findings.what: An 8B Lean prover built on Qwen3-8B. It makes training problems from the unsolved goals of failed proofs, corrects itself with compiler feedback, and averages checkpoints to keep diversity.
findings.steal: Mine dawnr's failed prover runs for their failing subgoals and add each, with its context, as a new and easier row; this grows the scarce prover-accepted data. Also average dawnr checkpoints after SFT and RL ((1-a)theta0 + a*theta). The Apache-2.0 8B weights could be measured as a Lean-leg helper.
findings.moves: Data scarcity; answer rate
findings.evidence: Self-correction (2 rounds) raised miniF2F pass@32 from 88.1% to 90.4% and PutnamBench from 43 to 57 solved. The 8B model reaches 84.6% pass@32 on miniF2F.
findings.risk: Training data includes DeepSeek-Prover-V2 outputs (allowed, but say so). Lean only. 8B is heavy on CPU.

findings.name: VerMCTS
findings.what: MCTS over program prefixes. The LLM proposes the next step, and Dafny or Coq checks each partial program to bound its value.
findings.steal: Reuse the MCTS loop with dawnr's t checker as the partial-program heuristic: check t prefixes (type check plus prover on the finished parts) and expand only the live branches, instead of independent whole samples.
findings.moves: Answer rate per token on CPU
findings.evidence: More than a 30% absolute increase in average pass@5000 tokens over repeated sampling across its Dafny and Coq suite.
findings.risk: dawnr's repos-verification.md already notes it. The baseline is CodeLlama-34B on A100s; t needs a prefix checker that is fast on CPU.

findings.name: OpenCodeReasoning
findings.licence: CC BY 4.0 (dataset card); problems keep their source licences
findings.what: 735,255 Python reasoning traces and solutions to 28,319 competitive-programming problems, all generated by DeepSeek R1.
findings.steal: Use it as distillation SFT for the 'write a right program' half, through dawnr's Python hand-back. First execute every solution against the problems' tests and keep only passing rows from MIT, Apache or CC-BY sources.
findings.moves: Answer rate (program correctness), data volume
findings.evidence: 735k samples; the card says R1 generated all outputs and does not state that they were execution-verified.
findings.risk: Model-generated by R1 (not on the banned list). The per-problem licences vary and must be filtered. Competitive-programming style differs from t.

findings.name: Type-constrained decoding (prefix automata)
findings.what: Decoding that admits only well-typed prefixes, through prefix automata, formalised for a simply typed language and extended to TypeScript.
findings.steal: Build a t prefix automaton for t's type system and combine it with CRANE switching, so the program region is both parseable and well typed.
findings.moves: Answer rate, only where ill-typed programs are a measurable share of failures
findings.evidence: Cuts compilation errors by more than half on HumanEval and MBPP, and raises functional correctness, across models including ones over 30B.
findings.risk: dawnr found syntax is not the bottleneck; first measure what share of t failures are type errors. Repo pushed Mar 2026.

findings.name: Seed-Coder-8B-Instruct / Reasoning
findings.what: An 8B code model trained on LLM-filtered code data, with a 64K-context Reasoning variant.
findings.steal: Add it to dawnr's base-model measurement for the t student and as a second, non-Qwen family for RL controls.
findings.moves: Answer rate; robustness of RL claims across model families
findings.evidence: LiveCodeBench (2410-2502): 24.7 vs 17.3 for Qwen2.5-Coder-7B; MBPP 85.2 vs 83.5; HumanEval 84.8 vs 88.4.
findings.risk: 8B is about twice the CPU cost of 4B. Python benchmarks may not transfer to t.

findings.name: F* PoPAI (type-based retrieval)
findings.licence: paper CC BY 4.0; dataset licence not found
findings.what: A corpus of 600K lines (32K definitions) of F* programs and proofs. Fine-tuned Phi-2 and StarCoder rival GPT-4, and type-based retrieval helps a lot.
findings.steal: Add retrieval by type and signature over dawnr's accepted rows: at generation time, insert the nearest proved t definitions with matching types as context.
findings.moves: Answer rate with scarce data
findings.evidence: Small fine-tuned models 'compare favorably with large language models (such as GPT-4)'; type-based retrieval 'boost[s] performance significantly'.
findings.risk: The dataset location and licence were not on the fetched page.

findings.name: Absolute Zero (deduction, abduction, induction tasks)
findings.what: Self-play with no data, where an executor checks three task types: predict the output, infer the input, and synthesize the program from examples.
findings.steal: Use dawnr's t interpreter to make free auxiliary rows (predict a t program's output, find an input that gives a stated output) and mix them into SFT as cheap, checked data.
findings.moves: Data scarcity
findings.evidence: Gains grow with size: 3B +5.7, 7B +10.2, 14B +13.2. Removing induction cut math from 38.4 to 33.3.
findings.risk: Small models gain least and plateau faster. Its executor is 'not secure'. A Llama-8B run produced unsafe 'uh-oh' text.

findings.name: Docling
findings.what: Local document converter for PDF, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX, HTML, EML/MSG and images, with layout, reading order, table structure and OCR, and output that keeps page numbers and bounding boxes.
findings.steal: Use it as an optional reader inside locallm/doc_read.py for scanned PDFs, tables, slides, spreadsheets and email, so each quoted sentence has a page and a box. pdftotext stays the default.
findings.moves: Breadth for ordinary people: scans and tables are refused today, and doc_read.py itself says Docling is what they need.
findings.evidence: Paper arXiv:2501.17887: median 0.79 s/page, mean 3.1 s/page on an 8-thread x86 CPU (MinerU 3.3, Marker 16+). Release v2.133.0 on 2026-10-03.
findings.risk: Large install (torch and layout models). Pages in the slowest 5% take 16.3 s on CPU. Keep it an optional extra.

findings.name: deepset/deberta-v3-base-squad2
findings.what: A 0.2B encoder that reads a question and returns the start and end offsets of an answer in the text, or no answer.
findings.steal: Put it in extract_docs.py as the span picker: it proposes character offsets inside the sentence the grammar chose, and the existing check that the span is in the source stays. A span model cannot write text that is not in the source.
findings.moves: Extraction quality: dawnr's grammar-held 4B extractor copied whole sentences and got 165/300 answerable exact on SQuAD 2.0.
findings.evidence: SQuAD 2.0 dev: 83.8 EM / 87.4 F1 at 0.2B parameters.
findings.risk: Trained on SQuAD (CC-BY-SA), so check the share-alike question. English only. The evaluation set overlaps dawnr's SQuAD panel, so measure on a different set.

findings.name: TAT-QA
findings.licence: CC-BY-4.0 (README; HF tag license:cc-by-4.0); code MIT
findings.what: Questions written by people over real financial reports that mix tables and text, with answers that are spans, several spans, counts, or arithmetic with the derivation shown.
findings.steal: Use it as training and evaluation data for 'questions with numbers in my documents': quote the cells or sentences, then compute the derivation in calc.py, and grade the result exactly.
findings.moves: Number questions and data scarcity: about 16.5k rows with human answers that can be checked exactly.
findings.evidence: 16,552 questions over 2,757 table-plus-text contexts.
findings.risk: Finance only and English only. Tables must be flattened into sentences or cells that the quote grammar can cite.

findings.name: FinQA
findings.what: Questions about financial reports, written by financial experts, each with a gold reasoning program in a small arithmetic language and the supporting facts.
findings.steal: Translate its programs into calc.py expressions and use them as training rows where the arithmetic is the check: quoted facts in, an exact result out.
findings.moves: Data for number answers with provenance, and a calc-mode benchmark that a program can grade.
findings.evidence: Abstract: 'written by financial experts', with gold programs. Corrected baseline is 61.24 execution accuracy.
findings.risk: Repository last pushed in 2022. Read the dataset terms beyond the MIT footer before training on it.

findings.name: PaddleOCR-VL-1.5
findings.what: A 0.9B document VLM that turns page images into markdown or JSON with layout polygons, tables, formulas and reading order, and runs on CPU through llama.cpp GGUF.
findings.steal: Use it as the recognizer for scans on the llama.cpp server dawnr already runs, with Tesseract as an independent second reader so a quote from a scan is shown only when both agree.
findings.moves: Scanned documents, which are refused today, and vision in the installed command.
findings.evidence: 94.5 on OmniDocBench v1.5. Released 2026-01-29. GGUF builds exist.
findings.risk: Speed of a 0.9B VLM per page on CPU is not measured. It is a model writing the source text, so quotes need an agreement check (see shifts).

findings.name: granite-docling-258M
findings.what: A 258M page-to-DocTags model (Idefics3 with SigLIP2) for tables, code, equations and full-page OCR, quantised for llama.cpp.
findings.steal: Use it as the lightweight table reader behind Docling for born-digital PDFs on low-end machines.
findings.moves: Tables in documents on CPU-only installs.
findings.evidence: FinTabNet TEDS 0.97 for structure and 0.96 with content. Full-page OCR F1 0.84.
findings.risk: English only (Japanese, Arabic and Chinese are experimental). Weak on general images (MMStar 0.30).

findings.name: wtpsplit (SaT)
findings.what: Sentence and paragraph segmentation in 85 languages that works without punctuation, with LoRA domain adapters and ONNX.
findings.steal: Use it as the multilingual splitter behind cite and extract, so a 'sentence' means the same thing in Thai, Japanese or a PDF without punctuation. Keep pySBD and UAX 29 as fallbacks.
findings.moves: Documents beyond English: the quote unit is the sentence, so a wrong split is a wrong quote.
findings.evidence: sat-12l-sm: 97.4 English F1 and 96.0 multilingual F1, against Punkt at 92.2 English. Release 2.2.2 on 2026-09-25.
findings.risk: A transformer on CPU is slower than rules; sat-3l is the small option (89.2 multilingual F1).

findings.name: TyDi QA
findings.what: About 204k information-seeking questions in 11 typologically diverse languages, with byte-offset minimal answer spans or NULL.
findings.steal: Use it as the multilingual panel for cite and extract (answerable and NULL), measured the same way the SQuAD 2.0 panel is now.
findings.moves: Documents are measured in English only.
findings.evidence: 11 languages. Questions were 'written by people who want to know the answer, but don't know the answer yet', so they were not translated or primed.
findings.risk: The passages are Wikipedia, not personal documents. GoldP leaves out Thai and Japanese.

findings.name: CUAD
findings.what: Expert-labelled clause spans in 510 real commercial contracts, shipped as PDF and TXT, in SQuAD 2.0 style.
findings.steal: Use it as an end-to-end PDF benchmark for dawnr extract: real PDFs go through doc_read, and a field is right only if its span matches the expert span.
findings.moves: Breadth: real PDFs and long documents instead of Wikipedia paragraphs. Also adds extraction rows.
findings.evidence: More than 13,000 labels, 41 clause categories, 510 contracts with PDFs included.
findings.risk: Legal English only. 33 of the 41 categories are yes/no presence, not a value.

findings.name: granite-embedding-97m-multilingual-r2
findings.what: A 97M multilingual embedding model with a 32k context, 384 dimensions and 200+ languages.
findings.steal: Use it as the CPU dense retriever next to BM25 in dawnr_retrieval for documents not in English.
findings.moves: Retrieval over a person's documents in many languages, on a CPU.
findings.evidence: 60.3 on MTEB Multilingual Retrieval, which the card calls the best open model under 100M, ahead by about 9.4 points.
findings.risk: Trained partly on 'IBM-generated synthetic data' from an unnamed generator. This is fine for weights dawnr uses, but not a data source.

findings.name: GLiNER2
findings.what: A 205M-340M encoder for schema-driven extraction (entities, classification, structured records) that returns character offsets and confidences.
findings.steal: Use it as a CPU field extractor for dawnr extract: the schema fields become labels and the output is offsets that are checked against the source, with no generation.
findings.moves: Extraction speed and span precision on CPU, without the 4B model.
findings.evidence: Paper arXiv:2507.18546: CrossNER average F1 0.590 vs GPT-4o 0.599; 163 ms CPU with 20 labels. Release v2.0.0 on 2026-08-24.
findings.risk: 118,636 of its 254k training rows were generated by GPT-4o. Use the weights only if that is allowed; never use its data. English only.

findings.name: Microsoft Recognizers-Text
findings.what: A rule-based recognizer for numbers, ordinals, percentages, ranges, currency, dimensions, temperature, dates and times, phone numbers and emails in about 10 languages.
findings.steal: Use it as the non-model check that a span 'reads as a number' or 'reads as a date' in extract_docs.py typed fields, in languages beyond English.
findings.moves: Typed fields and number questions beyond English, with a deterministic check.
findings.evidence: Full support for 10 languages (zh, en, fr, es, pt, de, it, tr, hi, nl). Last push 2026-04-17.
findings.risk: The Python port is labelled alpha; .NET is the primary implementation.

findings.name: quantulum3
findings.what: A quantity and unit parser that returns value, unit, entity, uncertainty and span offsets, including ranges.
findings.steal: Feed its output into a unit-consistency check in calc.py: the quoted quantity's unit must match the unit in the answer, with the arithmetic done in exact units.
findings.moves: Numeric and unit checks that are not a language model.
findings.evidence: Returns span offsets and uncertainties (for example ±0.1 and the range '12.8–13.0 TeV').
findings.risk: English only on the main branch. Its optional disambiguation classifier uses GloVe vectors; skip it.

findings.name: llguidance for quote grammars
findings.what: A constrained-decoding engine built into llama.cpp (LLAMA_LLGUIDANCE) that takes Lark, regex and JSON-schema grammars.
findings.steal: Compile the per-document quote grammar (any sentence, or a run of a sentence's words) as Lark through llguidance instead of large GBNF alternations, so cite and extract scale to long documents.
findings.moves: Cite and extract over long documents, where the sentence-alternation grammar grows with the document.
findings.evidence: About 50 µs of CPU per token for a 128k tokenizer; under 1% of masks take over 1 ms. dawnr's own measurement on t: 0.602 ms.
findings.risk: dawnr found llguidance does not accept its GBNF, so the grammars must be written in Lark. Not measured on grammars with thousands of sentences.

findings.name: ContractNLI
findings.licence: CC-BY-4.0 (project page and GitHub). The HF copy kiddothe2b/contract-nli is tagged CC-BY-NC-SA, so use the original.
findings.what: 607 NDAs, each with 17 hypotheses labelled entailed, contradicted or not mentioned, plus the evidence sentences.
findings.steal: Use it as a refusal and contradiction panel for cite: the shown sentence must be the evidence span, and 'not mentioned' must be refused.
findings.moves: Honest refusal when a document does not say something, including negation by exception.
findings.evidence: 607 contracts × 17 hypotheses with sentence-level evidence.
findings.risk: English NDAs only; a narrow domain.

findings.name: ParseBench
findings.what: A benchmark of document parsers on 2,078 enterprise pages, including content faithfulness (omissions and hallucinations) and visual grounding of each element.
findings.steal: Use its faithfulness and grounding subsets to choose dawnr's parser (pdftotext vs Docling vs a VLM) by measurement before shipping one.
findings.moves: Choosing a document reader by measurement; provenance back to page location.
findings.evidence: 1,211 documents, 2,078 pages, 169,011 rules. Grounding is scored by element pass rate.
findings.risk: The leaderboard does not list the open CPU parsers, so dawnr would run them itself.

findings.name: trafilatura
findings.licence: Apache-2.0 since v1.8.0 (README; older versions GPLv3+)
findings.what: Main-text and metadata extraction from HTML that removes navigation and boilerplate, with tables and comments optional.
findings.steal: Use it in ingest.py for saved web pages, so quotes come from the article and not from menus or footers.
findings.moves: Breadth for HTML documents.
findings.evidence: Best single tool by ROUGE-LSum mean F1 in Bevendorff et al. 2023 (README). Pushed 2026-10-02.
findings.risk: Pin version 1.8.0 or later to stay off the GPL releases. It adds lxml dependencies.

findings.name: CaMeL (Defeating Prompt Injections by Design)
findings.what: A privileged model turns only the trusted user query into a program; a custom interpreter runs it with capability labels on every value and checks a security policy before each tool call; untrusted data is read by a quarantined model and never changes control flow.
findings.steal: Extend dawnr's 'arguments were actually said' gate into capability tracking: tag each argument value with its source (user said / document / tool output), have the interpreter carry those tags, and write deterministic policies per tool, recording the tags in the certificate.
findings.moves: Tool calls and MCP safety; certificates (the provenance tags are replayable)
findings.evidence: 77% of AgentDojo tasks solved with provable security, against 84% with no defence (arXiv 2503.18813)
findings.risk: The authors say the interpreter 'likely contains bugs' and 'might not be fully secure'. It is a research artifact (3 commits), so reimplement the design rather than vendoring it.

findings.name: Catala + catala-examples
findings.what: A language for writing law as code with default logic, compiling to Python, Java, OCaml and C; it has a test runner and execution traces, and the example repo encodes French family and housing benefits, US tax code sections and Polish taxes.
findings.steal: Ship the compiled Python of the catala-examples programs as everyday checkers (benefits and tax sections). The model only fills in the facts each scope takes as input, quoted from what the person said, and the `clerk run --trace` JSON becomes the certificate a third party replays.
findings.moves: Breadth for ordinary people (tax and benefits questions); answer rate in that domain (the model writes facts, not programs or specs)
findings.evidence: Release 1.3.0 on 2026-10-01 added `clerk run --trace` JSON output and trace generation in the Java, Python and OCaml backends; 5,730 commits
findings.risk: The encoded laws are mostly French and only cover parts of US tax; each law needs upkeep every year; building requires an OCaml toolchain (ship the generated Python, not the compiler).

findings.name: sqlglot
findings.what: A SQL parser and optimizer with no dependencies, over 30 dialects; it resolves columns against a schema (qualify, annotate_types), computes semantic diffs between queries, and includes a Python executor.
findings.steal: Use it as the deterministic gate for 'SQL over your own tables': parse the model's SQL, reject anything that is not a single read-only SELECT, qualify it against the schema of the user's CSV or XLSX file, then run it in the sandbox and put the SQL and a hash of the table in the certificate.
findings.moves: Breadth (spreadsheets and tables for non-programmers); checked action
findings.evidence: No-dependency parser; the optimizer's qualify and annotate_types rules resolve columns against a schema; 8,403 commits
findings.risk: Checking syntax and schema does not make the query correct; it needs an agreement check (see QED) or execution checks.

findings.name: TaxCalcBench
findings.what: Personal income tax returns built from the tests of a deterministic tax engine; inputs are realistic W-2 and 1099 PDFs plus JSON, and expected outputs are IRS MeF XML.
findings.steal: Use it as the evaluation set for dawnr's document-plus-calculation path (extract the fields with their source sentences, then compute with Catala or exact arithmetic). Score strict accuracy and the refusal rate.
findings.moves: Breadth (high-stakes everyday computation); a public comparison against frontier models
findings.evidence: Version 2 (June 2026) has 50 cases for tax year 2025; the best is GPT-6 Sol with web search at 66% strict, and top models get 88-90% per line
findings.risk: Small (50 cases) and US federal only. Use it for evaluation only, never training (it is a benchmark).

findings.name: Language Models and Logic Programs for Trustworthy Tax Reasoning (legal_logic_programs)
findings.licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (code, as stated in the paper)
findings.what: A model parses a tax case into Prolog facts, the solver computes the tax, and the system abstains unless two independent parses agree; the paper scores it by break-even price per return, with errors and abstentions priced.
findings.steal: Adopt two independent formalizations that must agree before an answer is shown, for domains with no gold spec, and adopt the scoring that prices each refusal at the cost of the human alternative. Reimplement it; the CC BY-SA code is not copied.
findings.moves: Answer-rate measurement; gate design outside the provers
findings.evidence: o3 got 75 of 100 SARA cases; GPT-5 few-shot with gold statutes got 86 correct with a $15.78 break-even price per return, against a $270 average human preparer
findings.risk: CC BY-SA is share-alike, so take the idea only. The best results use closed models; the open models tested were 32B to 671B.

findings.name: Numbat
findings.what: A small scientific language where physical dimensions are static types, with first-class units, conversions with ->, assert_eq, a large prelude written in Numbat itself, and a WebAssembly build.
findings.steal: Make Numbat the units checker behind dawnr's calc: the model writes a Numbat expression, the type checker rejects dimension errors before evaluation, and the expression plus result go in the certificate. The WASM build serves dawnr's browser page.
findings.moves: Checked computation beyond arithmetic (units); breadth for ordinary questions
findings.evidence: Dimensions such as Length and Time act as types with inference; prelude covers SI, US Customary, Imperial, Nautical, Astronomical and Atomic units; runs as WASM at numbat.dev
findings.risk: It is a Rust dependency (Pint, BSD, is the pure-Python alternative). Check how it handles currency and dates before relying on it for money.

findings.name: CPMpy
findings.what: A Python constraint-modelling library over OR-Tools, Z3, Exact, Pumpkin, SCIP, HiGHS and PySAT, with companion explanation tooling (XCP-explain).
findings.steal: Add a constraint path for everyday scheduling, budgeting and assignment questions: the model writes a CPMpy model, the solver solves it, an independent check confirms the solution satisfies every constraint, and an unsatisfiable core names the constraint that failed in the refusal.
findings.moves: Checked computation (constraints and SMT); refusals that name the check
findings.evidence: Supports CP, ILP, SAT and SMT (Z3) backends; 1,990 commits
findings.risk: Checking a solution against the model does not prove the model matches the question; this path needs quoting or agreement checks like the other paths.

findings.name: DCP-Bench-Open (CP-Bench)
findings.what: 164 combinatorial problems (167 instances) for model-written constraint models in MiniZinc, CPMpy and OR-Tools, scored by whether the solution is feasible and optimal.
findings.steal: Use it as the test set for the CPMpy path and as seed problems for prover-free, solution-checked training rows.
findings.moves: Data (checkable rows outside the provers); measuring the constraint path
findings.evidence: CPMpy about 70% at baseline and 90.2% with inference-time methods; 10-sample solution majority voting added over 10%
findings.risk: Puzzle-style problems are not everyday questions. The license was read from the paper, so confirm it in the repo's LICENSE.

findings.name: Arctic-Text2SQL-R1-7B
findings.what: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct trained with GRPO using only execution correctness and syntax validity as rewards.
findings.steal: Copy the recipe: dawnr's prover acceptance (or SQL execution match) is the whole reward, with no shaped or model-judged reward. The weights could also serve as a teacher for the SQL path.
findings.moves: Answer rate (training recipe); SQL over a person's tables
findings.evidence: BIRD-test 68.5%, Spider-test 88.8%, Spider2.0-DK 15.6%
findings.risk: 7B is heavy on CPU. The training data sources are not stated on the card; the related OmniSQL/SynSQL-2.5M data (Apache-2.0) was partly generated by Llama 3.1, so it cannot be dawnr training data unless filtered by generator.

findings.name: QED prover (SQL query equivalence)
findings.what: A Rust decider for SQL query equivalence (VLDB 2024), built on Z3 and CVC5.
findings.steal: Gate SQL answers on agreement: two independently written queries (two samples, or a model and a template) must be proved equivalent by QED before the result is shown; when QED cannot decide, fall back to comparing executions on the user's table.
findings.moves: Checked SQL where no spec exists; the 'something that did not write it agrees' principle
findings.evidence: About 290 of about 440 Calcite rewrite cases are provable (about 66%); default SMT timeout 10 s
findings.risk: Input is a JSON intermediate form produced by a separate parser; 66 commits, research-grade; not every SQL feature is covered.

findings.name: FIDES (information-flow control for agents)
findings.what: A planner that puts integrity (trusted/untrusted) and confidentiality (public/private) labels on every value, propagates them through tool calls, and deterministically enforces policies before sensitive tools run, with primitives to hide or reveal values.
findings.steal: Use its label lattice and hide/reveal variables as the design for dawnr's MCP tool gate: document text and tool outputs enter as untrusted variables the planner cannot read, and a policy blocks writing tools whose arguments carry untrusted labels.
findings.moves: Tool-call and MCP safety; certificate content (labels)
findings.evidence: Repo is a tutorial notebook (5 commits); the design ships experimentally in Microsoft agent-framework-core as agent_framework.security (arXiv 2505.23643)
findings.risk: The notebook calls Azure OpenAI (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1); take the design, not the setup.

findings.name: AgentDojo
findings.what: A benchmark of agent tasks plus prompt-injection attacks, with pluggable defence pipelines, published at NeurIPS 2024.
findings.steal: Measure dawnr's tool gate (said-arguments plus capability labels) as a defence pipeline in AgentDojo and report utility alongside attack success, so it can be compared directly with CaMeL's 77% and Progent.
findings.moves: A measured claim for tool-call safety
findings.evidence: `pip install agentdojo`; CaMeL and Progent both report results on it
findings.risk: The tasks assume a strong planner model; a 4B model's utility may be low regardless of the gate.

findings.name: DABstep
findings.what: Multi-step data-analysis questions over a payments CSV and a fee manual, scored by exact match on numbers, yes/no answers, lists and 'Not Applicable'.
findings.steal: Use it as the evaluation for 'questions about my own spreadsheet': dawnr answers with SQL or calc plus quoted fee-manual rules and must refuse with 'Not Applicable' when the data cannot answer.
findings.moves: Breadth (tables and documents together); refusal quality
findings.evidence: 450 tasks plus 10 dev, split into easy and hard; answers rounded to specified decimals for exact scoring
findings.risk: Use it for evaluation only (it has a public leaderboard). The domain is payments, not household.

findings.name: s(CASP) and Blawx
findings.what: A goal-directed constraint answer-set reasoner that returns justification trees and natural-language explanations; Blawx is a block-based rules-as-code editor on top of it, aimed at non-programmers.
findings.steal: Use s(CASP) justification trees as the human-readable part of a rule-based certificate and refusal ('not eligible because condition X was not shown'), and Blawx's block editor as a model for letting non-programmers write or inspect rules.
findings.moves: Refusals that name the check; non-programmer audience
findings.evidence: Justification trees with the ?++ operator; about 10x faster than the original Ciao implementation; Blawx has 1,134 commits
findings.risk: Needs SWI-Prolog 8.5.6 or later; Blawx says it is 'not production-quality software'.

findings.name: MedCalc-Bench
findings.licence: CC-BY-SA 4.0 (repo); the HF v1.0 card says CC-BY-4.0
findings.what: 55 clinical calculators implemented as Python functions, with patient notes, questions, relevant entities and ground-truth explanations.
findings.steal: Learn the pattern for the dosage and medical-score domain: extract the entities with their source sentences from the note, then run a fixed calculator function. Use it for evaluation; train on it only if the licence conflict resolves to CC-BY.
findings.moves: Breadth (dosage and clinical calculations as checked computation)
findings.evidence: 10,543 training and 1,100 evaluation instances; v1.0 is flagged 'highly unreliable' and v1.2 fixed 12 calculator implementations
findings.risk: Share-alike licence (not on the allowed list); the two pages state the licence differently; it is medical, so it carries safety and liability weight.

findings.name: NeMo-Speech.cpp
findings.licence: Apache-2.0 for NVIDIA code, third-party parts keep their own terms (README); the models it runs are CC-BY-4.0 (Parakeet and Sortformer cards)
findings.what: NVIDIA's C++ runtime on ggml for Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3, Parakeet CTC 1.1B, Streaming Sortformer diarization and MagpieTTS. It exposes OpenAI-compatible transcription routes.
findings.steal: Ship it next to llama.cpp as the speech backend of the installed `dawnr` command, behind dawnr's existing local OpenAI-style API, so speech stops being a research harness.
findings.moves: Speech only in research harnesses; the local API; offline on CPU
findings.evidence: CPU: 27 ms per 160 ms chunk and 6x real time; Q8_0 quantization; OpenAI-compatible transcription subset plus realtime WebSocket
findings.risk: Young repo (22 commits). Word confidence is not documented. MagpieTTS licence not checked. The VoiceChat 11B and Translate 4B models are out of scope.

findings.name: NeMo Forced Aligner (method) + parakeet-ctc-0.6b
findings.licence: Paper: none stated. Weights nvidia/parakeet-ctc-0.6b: CC-BY-4.0 (model card). The NFA docs page states no licence.
findings.what: Viterbi alignment of a given text on a CTC model's log-probabilities. It gives token, word and segment timestamps and works on audio over an hour long.
findings.steal: Use it as the check for quotes from recordings: the model proposes a quote, Viterbi on CTC log-probs aligns it to the audio, and the certificate records start, end and per-word score. If alignment fails, the answer is refused. Reimplement the Viterbi in a few hundred lines rather than depend on NeMo.
findings.moves: Lets a quote from a recording carry its time, so speech gets the same quote check that documents have
findings.evidence: AMI meetings, ground-truth text: NFA precision 98.35% at RTF 149. MFA got 82.93% and aligned only 5 of 16 files. When the text came from ASR, NFA dropped to 85.65% precision and 71.09% recall.
findings.risk: English CTC model only. Parakeet weights are CC-BY, so the credit must ship. 600M parameters on CPU is slow for long audio.

findings.name: OvisOCR2
findings.what: An end-to-end document OCR model with 0.8B parameters, built on Qwen3.5-0.8B with SFT, RL and OPD. It outputs Markdown with formulas, tables and bounding boxes for image regions.
findings.steal: Run its GGUF in the same llama.cpp process to read scanned PDFs and photos into text. Check that text against an independent OCR reader (RapidOCR) before any quote from it is accepted.
findings.moves: Documents for ordinary people: scanned pages, photos of letters, forms
findings.evidence: OmniDocBench v1.6 overall 96.58, top of the leaderboard (Qwen3-VL-235B scores 89.78 there); 25 quantized variants for llama.cpp
findings.risk: Released July 2026. Its training data mixes real and synthetic data from an unnamed generator, which matters only if dawnr fine-tunes on its outputs. The card says to verify its output by hand.

findings.name: sherpa-onnx
findings.what: An offline speech toolkit on ONNX Runtime. It covers ASR (Parakeet, Moonshine and others), VAD, open-vocabulary keyword spotting, speaker diarization, TTS and word timestamps, on Linux, macOS, Windows, Raspberry Pi and WASM.
findings.steal: Use it as the fallback speech layer for machines where ggml speech is not built. Its open-vocabulary KWS (3 to 19 MB, keywords given as text, no retraining) would serve as dawnr's wake word.
findings.moves: Speech and wake word in the installed command; install across platforms
findings.evidence: v1.13.8 released 2026-09-10. The English gigaspeech KWS encoder is 4.6 MB in int8. Diarization confidence is exposed in recent releases.
findings.risk: Each pretrained model has its own licence. The fetched page states no licence for the gigaspeech KWS model, and GigaSpeech data terms must be checked.

findings.name: Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3
