findings.what: A FastConformer-TDT recognizer with 600M parameters for 25 European languages. It gives timestamps for words, segments and characters and handles up to 24 minutes of audio with full attention.
findings.steal: Replace whisper.cpp as the default recognizer. It is a transducer, not a free-running text decoder, it gives word times natively, and it covers non-English speech.
findings.moves: Speech; breadth beyond English
findings.evidence: Average WER 6.34% on the Open ASR leaderboard; LibriSpeech clean 1.93%. Trained on 10k hours of human-transcribed audio plus 660k hours of pseudo-labeled Granary.
findings.risk: Pseudo-labels came from a model. The card says it is optimized for NVIDIA GPUs, so CPU speed has to be measured (NeMo-Speech.cpp reports 6x real time). The attribution must ship.

findings.name: Entropy-based word confidence for CTC and RNN-T
findings.licence: arXiv non-exclusive distribution licence (paper; the method is free to reimplement)
findings.what: Word confidence for CTC and RNN-T recognizers without training: per-frame entropy is normalized and aggregated per word.
findings.steal: Compute a confidence for each transcript word from the Parakeet logits and write it into the certificate. Low-confidence words inside a quoted span make the quote refused, and the refusal names the word.
findings.moves: Gives a checkable confidence per word, so a refusal can name the word that failed
findings.evidence: Up to 2x (Conformer-CTC) and 4x (Conformer-RNN-T) better than max-probability at detecting wrong words on LibriSpeech
findings.risk: The confidence is not calibrated for every domain, so a threshold must be set on held-out audio.

findings.name: Silero VAD
findings.what: A voice activity detector of about 2 MB at 8 and 16 kHz.
findings.steal: Gate every recognizer input with it, so silence never reaches the decoder (the main trigger of invented ASR text). Record the speech spans in the certificate.
findings.moves: Makes speech output safer to trust, in the installed command
findings.evidence: Under 1 ms per chunk on one CPU thread; ONNX up to 4-5x faster than PyTorch
findings.risk: The README gives no numeric accuracy. Threshold tuning is needed for noisy rooms.

findings.name: RapidOCR
findings.licence: Apache-2.0 code; converted PaddleOCR models redistributed under Apache-2.0 (README)
findings.what: PaddleOCR detection and recognition models converted to ONNX. They run on ONNX Runtime or OpenVINO and give a box, text and score for each line.
findings.steal: Make it the second reader that does not depend on the first: a quote from a scanned page counts only if the VLM's text and RapidOCR's line text agree, and the certificate stores the line box and score. docTR (Apache-2.0 code and weights, per-word boxes and confidence) is the alternative.
findings.moves: Documents, as an independent check on a model's reading
findings.evidence: Line-level box plus confidence. Upstream PP-OCRv6 claims +4.6% detection and +5.1% recognition over v5, with 50 languages in one model.
findings.risk: The default models are Chinese and English, and other scripts need other models. The release date was not visible.

findings.name: Florence-2-base
findings.what: A vision model with 0.23B parameters. Its task prompts include object detection, OCR_WITH_REGION and caption-to-phrase grounding.
findings.steal: Use it as a cheap independent checker: every object or text a VLM claims to see must be grounded to a box by Florence-2, or the claim is refused and the refusal names the ungrounded noun.
findings.moves: Vision moves out of the research harness, and OWLv2 is not the only check
findings.evidence: Zero-shot COCO detection 34.7 mAP; RefCOCO val 53.9%. Trained on FLD-5B (5.4B annotations, 126M images).
findings.risk: Released in 2023 with modest grounding accuracy. FLD-5B annotations were partly made by models (not stated on the card).

findings.name: Woodpecker (method)
findings.what: Corrects VLM hallucinations in five stages: extract key concepts, form questions, validate them with GroundingDINO and VQA, write claims, then correct the answer.
findings.steal: Reuse the pipeline shape without its OpenAI step. Nouns are extracted deterministically, an open-vocabulary detector validates each one, and claims that fail are refused. Measure it on AMBER (Apache-2.0, an LLM-free hallucination benchmark).
findings.moves: Vision answers trustworthy by an independent check
findings.evidence: POPE +30.66 points for MiniGPT-4 and +24.33 for mPLUG-Owl
findings.risk: No licence, and it uses the OpenAI API for extraction and correction, so neither can be copied.

findings.name: olmOCR 2 unit-test rewards (method)
findings.licence: Code Apache-2.0 (repo). olmOCR-mix-1025 and synthmix-1025 Apache-2.0. olmOCR-Bench ODC-BY-1.0.
findings.what: GRPO on a 7B OCR model where the reward is the fraction of binary deterministic unit tests passed: text presence and absence, reading order, tables, math.
findings.steal: Apply the recipe to dawnr's document reader: its quote and extraction checks become the reward for a small model. Use olmOCR-Bench's 7,010 deterministic tests as an evaluation set only.
findings.moves: The answer rate on documents, and data scarcity
findings.evidence: Synthetic data plus RLVR took olmOCR-Bench from 78.5 to 82.4. Synthmix is 2,186 pages and 30,381 tests at about $0.12 per page.
findings.risk: The synthmix HTML was written by Claude Sonnet 4, and bench tests by Gemini Flash 2.0 and Claude 3.7, so both are evaluation only and never training data.

findings.name: Moonshine streaming small
findings.licence: MIT (model card); legacy non-English models are under a non-commercial community licence (README)
findings.what: A streaming ASR model of 123M parameters (v2 tiny 34M, medium 245M) for edge CPUs.
findings.steal: The low-latency English recognizer for live dictation and the wake-then-listen loop on weak laptops, with Parakeet kept for transcripts that need to be quoted.
findings.moves: Speech on ordinary and weak hardware
findings.evidence: Average WER 7.84%; LibriSpeech clean 2.49%; RTFx 566; tiny int8 WER 12.81 vs 12.72
findings.risk: It has an autoregressive decoder and so can invent text (sherpa-onnx v1.13.5 fixed hallucination on silence). Avoid the non-English legacy models (non-commercial).

findings.name: Streaming Sortformer 4spk v2
findings.what: A streaming speaker diarizer of 117M parameters for up to 4 speakers.
findings.steal: Attach a speaker label and time span to every quote from a meeting recording, run through NeMo-Speech.cpp. pyannote community-1 (weights CC-BY-4.0, gated) is the alternative.
findings.moves: Who said it, for quotes from recordings
findings.evidence: DER 6.57% on CALLHOME 2-speaker, 12.44% on CALLHOME 4-speaker, 13.24% on DIHARD III; latency configurable from 0.32 s to 30.4 s
findings.risk: Degrades with 5 or more speakers. Only GPU numbers are given.

findings.name: Kokoro-82M
findings.what: A StyleTTS2 voice with 82M parameters: 54 voices in 8 languages.
findings.steal: Use it as the read-aloud voice for answers and refusals for people who do not read easily, beside or instead of Piper.
findings.moves: Usable by everyone (accessibility)
findings.evidence: v1.0 released 2025-01-27; trained on a few hundred hours for about 1,000 GPU hours
findings.risk: The card says the training data includes synthetic audio from closed commercial TTS models, so the provenance is weaker than the Apache tag. The card gives no CPU speed.

findings.name: openWakeWord (method)
findings.what: Wake-word models trained only on synthetic TTS speech of the phrase, with about 30k hours of negative audio.
findings.steal: Train dawnr's own wake word the same way, using Kokoro or Piper speech of the phrase and permissive negative audio. Do not use the shipped non-commercial models.
findings.moves: Wake word in the installed command without a non-commercial dependency
findings.evidence: Target under 0.5 false accepts per hour and under 5% false rejects; 15-20 models run in real time on one Raspberry Pi 3 core
findings.risk: Last release v0.6.0 (Feb 2024). The negative data must be permissively licensed.

findings.name: Grounding DINO / LLMDet
findings.what: Open-vocabulary detectors that find any phrase as boxes. LLMDet adds co-training on detailed captions.
findings.steal: Use as a stronger check than Florence-2 when it is too weak: a VLM claim about an object passes only if the detector finds it above a threshold.
findings.moves: An independent check on what a model says it sees
findings.evidence: LLMDet LVIS minival 44.7 AP (Swin-T) to 51.1 AP (Swin-L); Grounding DINO-T 48.4 AP zero-shot on COCO with a CPU mode; LLMDet is in transformers 4.55+
findings.risk: LLMDet's GroundingCap-1M captions were written by a fine-tuned LLaVA-OneVision-Qwen2-0.5B. Swin backbones are slow on CPU.

findings.name: PaddleOCR-VL
findings.what: A document parser of about 1B parameters (NaViT encoder and ERNIE-4.5-0.3B) for 109 languages. It outputs element bounding boxes, tables, formulas and charts.
findings.steal: Use it as the non-English document reader, so the document check stops being measured in English only.
findings.moves: Documents beyond English
findings.evidence: 109 languages; released 2025-10-16; PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 reports 96.3% on OmniDocBench v1.6; OpenVINO CPU speed-up 5.2x
findings.risk: The card says it was trained partly on proprietary datasets. The Paddle stack is heavy, and there is no llama.cpp path on the fetched page.

findings.name: Jan (desktop app on Tauri + llama.cpp)
findings.licence: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE, Copyright 2025 Menlo Research; attribution requested in user-facing docs)
findings.what: Offline ChatGPT-style desktop app built on Tauri and llama.cpp, with an OpenAI-compatible server on localhost:1337 and MCP.
findings.steal: Take Jan's Tauri shell: its model download/hardware-detect screens and how it packages llama-server. dawnr's bin/dawnr and page become a native app with .exe, .dmg, AppImage, .deb and Flatpak builds, as a new desktop/ directory.
findings.moves: Install is a shell script; people who do not use a terminal
findings.evidence: Ships jan.exe, jan.dmg, AppImage, .deb and Flatpak; minimum is macOS 13.6+ with 8 GB RAM; pushed 2026-10-05
findings.risk: Large TypeScript codebase to trim. The provers (.NET Dafny, Lean, Rocq) still need their own packaging per OS. Attribution is requested.

findings.name: DFlash block-diffusion drafters
findings.licence: MIT (GitHub licence field; README states MIT)
findings.what: Speculative decoding where a small block-diffusion drafter proposes a whole block of tokens in one pass, conditioned on the target model's hidden states.
findings.steal: Use the released drafter for Qwen3.5-4B through its llama.cpp backend in dawnr's serve path. Measure tokens/s on the CPU box and the 4080 before turning it on by default.
findings.moves: CPU speed, which gives more prove-and-repair attempts per question inside a fixed time budget (and so the answer rate)
findings.evidence: README lists drafters for Qwen3.5 4B/9B/27B/35B-A3B and llama.cpp, vLLM, SGLang and MLX backends. Paper (arXiv 2602.06036, ICML 2026) claims over 6x lossless speedup, up to 2.5x over EAGLE-3. v0.1.0 released 2026-08-18.
findings.risk: Speedups were measured on GPUs, and CPU gain is unknown. The drafter must be retrained if dawnr fine-tunes the 4B away from base Qwen3.5. The training code was not shown in the README.

findings.name: SuffixDecoding (Arctic Inference)
findings.what: Model-free speculative decoding that keeps suffix trees of prompts and earlier outputs and drafts long repeated spans from them.
findings.steal: Port the suffix-tree drafter idea to dawnr's repair loop (re-asking with prover errors) and to quoted-answer generation, using llama.cpp's speculative hook. Keep a per-question tree of the earlier attempts.
findings.moves: CPU latency of repair loops and of quote-heavy document answers
findings.evidence: Up to 5.3x faster on agentic workloads (SWE-Bench, Text-to-SQL); 2.8x over EAGLE-2/3; 1.9x over Token Recycling; NeurIPS 2025 spotlight
findings.risk: The reference code is a vLLM (GPU) plugin, so the port to llama.cpp is ours to write and maintain.

findings.name: wllama v3
findings.what: llama.cpp compiled to WebAssembly, with WebGPU offload, multimodal and tool calling, running fully in a browser tab.
findings.steal: Build a zero-install 'dawnr in a tab' for the checks that are pure code (quote, extract, exact arithmetic, tool-argument release). The model runs via wllama, and the same GGUF is split into 512 MB chunks.
findings.moves: Zero-install reach for people who do not program; the browser page
findings.evidence: Release 3.8.1 on 2026-10-02. Hard 2 GB per-file ArrayBuffer limit (split with llama-gguf-split). Multi-thread needs COOP/COEP headers.
findings.risk: A 4B Q4 model is about 2.5 GB, a heavy first download. The provers cannot follow into the tab (see z3-solver and jsCoq), so the program check stays native.

findings.name: cargo-dist (dist)
findings.what: Release tool that builds and hosts artifacts and generates shell, PowerShell, MSI, Homebrew and npm installers plus its own CI, including for non-Rust apps.
findings.steal: Replace dawnr's hand-written install.sh with dist-generated installers, adding PowerShell/MSI for native Windows without WSL and a Homebrew tap, plus a machine-readable release manifest that the certificate can cite.
findings.moves: Install is a shell script for Linux, macOS and WSL only
findings.evidence: Generates shell, PowerShell, MSI, Homebrew and npm installers and GitHub Actions CI; pushed 2026-10-05
findings.risk: The provers' own toolchains (dotnet, elan, opam) do not fit a single-binary model; they may need a separate 'dawnr provers install' step.

findings.name: Tauri sidecars
findings.what: Tauri's mechanism to bundle external binaries per target triple and spawn them, with an allowlist of arguments in capability files.
findings.steal: Ship llama-server and the prover binaries as sidecars ('externalBin'). Lock their arguments with the regex validators in capabilities/default.json, which matches dawnr's rule that tool calls run only with stated arguments.
findings.moves: Desktop install; sandboxing of spawned checkers
findings.evidence: Each binary must carry its target-triple suffix (e.g. -x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu); permission is shell:allow-execute with static or regex-validated args
findings.risk: The prover runtimes are large, so the app grows to gigabytes.

findings.name: Handy
findings.licence: MIT (README; name, logo and brand assets excluded)
findings.what: Offline push-to-talk app: press a shortcut, speak, and the transcript is pasted into whatever app is focused. Built with Tauri and ggml, using Silero VAD and Parakeet V3 on CPU.
findings.steal: Take its global-hotkey, record and paste loop (Rust/Tauri) as dawnr's 'ask anywhere' entry point. A spoken question goes to dawnr, and the checked answer (or the named refusal) is pasted back.
findings.moves: Accessible interface for people who do not use a terminal; speech in the product
findings.evidence: 32.9k stars is not evidence. Concrete facts: distributed via direct download, Homebrew, winget and APT; Parakeet V3 runs on CPU with automatic language detection.
findings.risk: The brand cannot be reused. Accessibility permissions differ per OS (macOS needs an accessibility grant).

findings.name: PocketPal AI
findings.what: React Native phone app running GGUF models via llama.cpp, published on the App Store and Google Play, with in-app Hugging Face download and a tokens/s benchmark.
findings.steal: Fork it for a dawnr phone client that runs the pure-code checks (quote, extract, arithmetic) on the phone. Its benchmark screen can report whether a device is fast enough.
findings.moves: Breadth for ordinary people (phones); hardware coverage
findings.evidence: Metal on iOS; OpenCL/Adreno and NPU on Android; ONNX Runtime TTS; 11 UI languages; pushed 2026-10-05
findings.risk: No provers on phones, so the program answers need a paired desktop or box. App-store review and upkeep fall on the operator.

findings.name: z3-solver (npm)
findings.licence: MIT (upstream Z3 LICENSE.txt in Z3Prover/z3; the npm README itself states none)
findings.what: Z3 compiled to WebAssembly with high-level (Z3Py-like) and low-level TypeScript bindings for browsers and Node.
findings.steal: Run t's SMT-level checks (e.g. spec-consistency or arithmetic side conditions) inside the browser page, so a third party can replay part of a certificate client-side with nothing installed.

findings.evidence: Version 5.2.0. Needs SharedArrayBuffer with COOP/COEP headers. Chrome 92+, Firefox 89+, Safari 15.2+.
findings.risk: This is not Dafny, Verus or Lean: Dafny's .NET-in-browser path is unproven, so only checks dawnr can lower to raw SMT replay in a tab.

findings.name: llamafile 0.10
findings.licence: Apache-2.0 (LICENSE, Mozilla Foundation); llama.cpp/whisper.cpp changes MIT
findings.what: One executable (Cosmopolitan APE) that bundles llama.cpp, GGUF weights and default args and runs on macOS, Linux, BSD and Windows.
findings.steal: Publish a 'dawnr-lite.llamafile' holding the published 4B GGUF plus an .args file (-m /zip/...) for the no-prover modes. That gives people a download-and-double-click trial.
findings.moves: Install friction; first-run for non-programmers
findings.evidence: Release 0.10.6 on 2026-09-15. Windows executables are capped at 4 GB. Weights are embedded with zipalign and referenced as /zip/.
findings.risk: The 4 GB Windows cap. It cannot carry the provers or Python checks, so it is a taster, not the product.

findings.name: Granite-4.0-H-Tiny
findings.what: A 7B-total, 1B-active hybrid Mamba2/MoE model (36 Mamba2 + 4 attention layers) with 128K context.
findings.steal: Add it to the base-model ladder as a CPU-speed candidate: with 1B active parameters per token it may decode several times faster than the dense 4B on the consumer box. Measure it under the gate on the clean-182 panel.
findings.moves: CPU latency; base-model choice by measurement
findings.evidence: HumanEval pass@1 83, MBPP 80, BFCL v3 57.65; 64 experts, 6 active
findings.risk: About 14 GB at BF16, so it needs Q4 to fit RAM. 'Internal synthetic data' in its SFT has an unnamed source (fine for weights we use, not for distilling as data). Contamination audit owed.

findings.name: ik_llama.cpp
findings.what: A llama.cpp fork adding IQ_K and trellis (KT) quants, row-interleaved formats, faster CPU prompt processing and MoE offload controls (--cpu-moe, auto-fit to VRAM).
findings.steal: Benchmark dawnr's 4B in IQ4_K / IQ4_KT against mainline Q4_K_M on the Acer Nitro box. Prompt processing speed dominates long document questions, so adopt it only if the gain is real.
findings.moves: CPU speed on long document prompts; small-GPU MoE offload
findings.evidence: Adds IQ2_K-IQ6_K and IQ1_KT-IQ4_KT, plus Hadamard transforms for the K/V cache; pushed 2026-10-05
findings.risk: The README gives no head-to-head numbers; a fork drifts from upstream, and its quant files do not load in mainline.

findings.name: WebLLM
findings.what: In-browser LLM engine compiled with MLC/TVM to WebGPU kernels, with an OpenAI-style API.
findings.steal: An alternative to wllama for the browser tab on GPU-equipped machines. Its OpenAI-style API lets dawnr's existing page code talk to it unchanged.
findings.moves: Zero-install browser reach
findings.evidence: Retains up to 80% of native performance on the same device (abstract); pushed 2026-10-03
findings.risk: Models need MLC compilation, not GGUF. WebGPU on Linux is not shipped by any major browser yet (web.dev).

findings.name: transformers.js v4
findings.what: ONNX models in the browser, Node, Deno and Bun on WASM or WebGPU, with fp32/fp16/q8/q4 dtypes. Pipelines cover ASR, TTS, embeddings and document QA.
findings.steal: Use it for the browser tab's small non-LLM parts (sentence embeddings for document retrieval, Moonshine/Parakeet ONNX ASR), not for the 4B.
findings.moves: Browser page breadth (speech and retrieval in the tab)
findings.evidence: Version 4.3.0; q8 is the WASM default, fp32 the WebGPU default
findings.risk: Duplicates what the native path already does; another runtime to keep in step.

findings.name: Moonshine Voice
findings.licence: MIT for code and all streaming and English models (LICENSE); legacy non-English non-streaming models are under the non-commercial Moonshine Community License
findings.what: On-device streaming speech-to-text, intent recognition and TTS, for Python, JS/WASM, iOS, Android and Raspberry Pi.
findings.steal: Use the MIT streaming English models as the low-latency 'listen' option on weak CPUs and in the browser tab. Skip the non-commercial legacy models entirely.
findings.moves: Speech in the installed command and on phones/Pi
findings.evidence: Sizes range down to about 1 MB; some variants claim higher accuracy than Whisper Large V3 (README; no table was on the fetched page)
findings.risk: Mixed licences need a per-model check. The accuracy claim was unquantified on the page fetched.

findings.name: AnythingLLM
findings.what: Desktop and Docker 'chat with your documents' app with drag-and-drop upload, source citations, a no-code agent builder, MCP, and connectors for Ollama, LM Studio and any llama.cpp model.
findings.steal: Study its document-upload and citation UI as the reference for dawnr's page. Also register dawnr's OpenAI-style API as a provider it can select, so its users get checked, word-for-word answers without leaving their app.
findings.moves: Documents for ordinary people; distribution through an existing user base
findings.evidence: Desktop for Mac/Windows/Linux plus an open-source Android app; PDF, TXT and DOCX supported
findings.risk: Its citations are model-asserted, not verified, so any UI copied must still show dawnr's refusals plainly.

findings.name: BitNet b1.58 2B4T + bitnet.cpp
findings.what: Native ternary-weight LLMs with a dedicated CPU runtime.
findings.steal: Track it as the long-run CPU path. If a ternary coder of about 4B appears, it would fit phones and old laptops. For now, run one gate measurement of the 2B4T as a speed floor, not a candidate.
findings.moves: Ordinary hardware, energy and latency
findings.evidence: 0.4 GB non-embedding memory; 29 ms/token CPU decode vs 65 ms for Qwen2.5-1.5B. bitnet.cpp gives 2.37x-6.17x x86 speedup with 71.9-82.2% energy cut. Parallel kernels (Jan 2026) add 1.15x-2.1x.
findings.risk: The card says research use, not production. No ternary model of dawnr's quality class exists, and it needs its own runtime.

findings.name: ReasoningLab (code-correctness probe before generation)
findings.licence: Apache-2.0 (repo README / GitHub licence field); paper arXiv 2606.14530 CC BY 4.0
findings.what: Linear probe on the final-prompt hidden state of Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 that predicts, before any token is generated, whether the first-attempt code will be correct.
findings.steal: Take its hidden-state extraction and probe training. Retrain the probe on Qwen3.5-4B states, labelled for free by dawnr's own prover pass/fail logs, and use it only to share out compute: more samples, escalate to 9B, or skip early. It never releases or blocks an answer.
findings.moves: Answer rate under a fixed CPU budget (most of the 182 are refused; spend samples where proof is likely)
findings.evidence: Held-out AUC 0.881 ± 0.008 on 444 LiveCodeBench tasks; 0.842 after removing prompt length, vs a 0.657 length-only baseline (arXiv 2606.14530 abstract)
findings.risk: Measured on tests passing, not on proof plus spec completeness; Qwen3.5 GGUF hidden states would need llama.cpp eval callbacks or an HF copy; single-author repo, last push 2026-07-16

findings.name: MAPIE (conformal prediction and risk control)
findings.what: Python library for conformal prediction and distribution-free risk control, including Learn Then Test and precision/recall guarantees.
findings.steal: Use Learn Then Test or precision control to set the thresholds where dawnr's checker is weaker than a proof: the document-quote retrieval score, extraction field acceptance and the probe's routing cut-off. Ship the calibrated alpha with each release, e.g. 'wrong-answer rate ≤ 5% at 95% confidence on the calibration set'.
findings.moves: Calibration of non-proof answers (documents, extraction), and a stated, measured error bound for everyone instead of an adjective
findings.evidence: v1.5.0 released 2026-08-05; README lists risk control with probabilistic guarantees, LTT calibration and exchangeability tests (new in 2026)
findings.risk: Guarantees need exchangeable labelled calibration data per domain, and English-only document sets limit what can be claimed; scikit-learn dependency

findings.name: model-signing (sigstore/model-transparency, OpenSSF Model Signing)
findings.what: CLI and library that sign a model directory as a Sigstore bundle (DSSE envelope with an in-toto statement of per-file digests), with Sigstore, private-key, certificate or PKCS#11 signing.
findings.steal: Sign every released GGUF plus its row manifest with `model_signing sign` in key mode. Have install.sh and `dawnr` verify before loading, and record the signature digest in each answer certificate so a replay names the exact weights.
findings.moves: Trust chain from installed weights to each certificate; the spaceship goal
findings.evidence: Releases v1.0.0 to v1.1.1 (2025-10-10, adds PKCS#11, BLAKE3, private Sigstore trust config); repo pushed 2026-10-05
findings.risk: Python dependency in the installer path; Sigstore keyless mode needs network (use key mode offline)

findings.name: Tessera (tile-based transparency log)
findings.what: Go library for append-only tile-based transparency logs with POSIX/GCP/AWS storage, C2SP witness cosigning and offline inclusion proofs.
findings.steal: Run a POSIX-backed log as static files (e.g. a GitHub Pages tree) that records hashes of released weights, row sets, held-out panels and published certificates. Each certificate then carries an inclusion proof, so a third party can check offline that the claim was published and never rewritten.
findings.moves: Third-party replay; makes contamination and panel audits tamper-evident
findings.evidence: v1.0.4 released 2026-07-16; production-ready since v0.2.0; offline proofs once a checkpoint is published
findings.risk: Go service to maintain; witnesses must be found (Sigsum's are an option, BSD per its docs)

findings.name: LM-Polygraph
findings.what: Framework of 40+ uncertainty estimators for LLM generation (token entropy, claim-conditioned probability, semantic entropy, Mahalanobis, EigenScore) with a benchmark.
findings.steal: Take the white-box estimators (claim-conditioned probability, mean token entropy) as extra cheap features for the routing probe and for ranking document-answer candidates before the quote check. Use its benchmark protocol (PRR) to report how well the score sorts proved from refused.
findings.moves: Answer rate (sample ranking) and calibration without an LLM judge
findings.evidence: v0.7.0 released 2026-05-04; examples run Qwen2.5-0.5B and Llama-3.1-8B locally
findings.risk: HF/PyTorch based, not llama.cpp; some methods (p(True), verbalized) are LLM self-judges and must be excluded

findings.name: Generative Prediction Sets (GPS)
findings.what: Conformal method that calibrates the minimum number of samples needed to get an admissible output from a black-box generator, giving a coverage guarantee (tested on code with pass-all-tests as admissibility).
findings.steal: Set admissibility to 'proved by the gate'. Calibrate per-domain k, the number of samples to draw before refusing, from dawnr's logs, so 'we tried k and none proved' is a calibrated statement rather than a fixed budget.
findings.moves: Answer rate per CPU second and an honest refusal rate
findings.evidence: Submitted 2025-03-13, revised 2025-06-16; validity guarantee on code and math across several LLMs
findings.risk: Paper only (CC BY-SA text, re-implement from the description); guarantee assumes exchangeable problems

findings.name: Croissant + RAI vocabulary (mlcroissant)
findings.licence: Apache-2.0 code (README); spec text CC BY-ND 4.0
findings.what: MLCommons JSON-LD dataset metadata format, read by Hugging Face, Kaggle and OpenML, with a Responsible-AI extension.
findings.steal: Publish dawnr's prover-accepted rows with a Croissant file. Set rai:machineAnnotationTools to the provers and versions, rai:dataCollection to the teacher models (which must be permissive), and rai:dataLimitations to the clean-182 exclusion, then validate with mlcroissant in CI.
findings.moves: Data trust and reuse; makes the scarce rows citable and auditable
findings.evidence: v1.1.1 released 2026-10-05; RAI spec 1.0 (2024-03-06) defines rai:machineAnnotationTools, rai:dataCollectionRawData, rai:personalSensitiveInformation
findings.risk: Spec text is No-Derivatives (use it, don't fork it); the metadata is only as honest as the pipeline that fills it

findings.name: ConStat (performance-based contamination test)
findings.what: Statistical test (bootstrap, no judge model) for whether a model's score on a benchmark is inflated relative to a matched reference benchmark.
findings.steal: Run it on dawnr vN and the base model, comparing the clean-182 against a freshly written, difficulty-matched reference set. This tests whether the base model's pretraining, which row audits cannot see, inflates the panel.
findings.moves: Contamination audit beyond dawnr's own rows (the 9/21 finding was row-side only)
findings.evidence: Uses bootstrap over accuracy with a random-model baseline; tested on GSM8K, MMLU, ARC, HellaSwag with 20+ reference models
findings.risk: Stale (last push 2024-07-29); the paper's reference sets were rephrased by a GPT model, so dawnr must write its own reference set, and only for evaluation

findings.name: Letta memory blocks
findings.what: Agent memory as labelled, size-limited text blocks (label, description, value, limit, read_only) that are always in context and that the user can read and edit through the API.
findings.steal: Copy the block schema for a per-person ~/.dawnr/memory file. Each entry holds the person's own sentence plus source and date, with a read_only flag and a character limit. Recall goes through the existing word-for-word quote check, so memory answers carry the same certificate.
findings.moves: Breadth for ordinary people (local, inspectable personalisation)
findings.evidence: letta 0.16.8 released 2026-05-14, repo pushed 2026-09-10; blocks have a read_only field and full-replace updates via API
findings.risk: Letta itself is a server platform (too heavy to ship); take only the schema and idea. Its agents rewrite memory with the LLM, which dawnr must not allow

findings.name: AlgoVeri
findings.what: 77 classical algorithms with aligned vericoding tasks in Dafny, Verus and Lean, plus evaluation code (ICML 2026).
findings.steal: Add it as a cross-prover held-out evaluation for t (after a heldout_audit against rows), to measure per-prover answer rate on the same problems and pick the order of the seven provers.
findings.moves: Reproducible evaluation; prover routing for answer rate
findings.evidence: Gemini-3 Flash: 40.3% Dafny, 24.7% Verus, 7.8% Lean on the same 77 problems
findings.risk: Who wrote the specs is not stated (check before training; use for evaluation); small (77)

findings.name: c2pa-unstructured-text
findings.what: Rust crate implementing C2PA 2.4 manifest embedding in plain text as invisible Unicode variation selectors, with hard binding, so provenance survives copy and paste.
findings.steal: Optionally embed a C2PA manifest that points to the answer certificate digest when a user copies a dawnr answer out of the page or CLI, so the pasted text still names its check. Keep it off by default.
findings.moves: Certificates that travel with answers for non-programmers
findings.evidence: v0.2.0 released 2026-08-02; implements C2PA spec 2.4 text binding
findings.risk: Single maintainer, new; invisible characters can be stripped or can upset screen readers and diffs; spec says use only when no other embedding works

findings.name: Carcara (Alethe SMT proof checker)
findings.what: Rust checker and elaborator for Alethe-format SMT proofs produced by cvc5 and veriT (TACAS 2023).
findings.steal: For provers that can call cvc5 (Frama-C/Why3, SPARK, optionally Dafny/Boogie), emit Alethe proofs and check them with Carcara in the certificate replay. 'Proved' then rests on a small checker, not on the solver's say-so.
findings.moves: Spaceship-grade trust; makes the replay independent of SMT solver bugs
findings.evidence: Repo pushed 2026-10-04 (last tagged release carcara-1.1.0, 2023-08-29); needs Rust 1.93+
findings.risk: Z3, the default for Dafny/Verus/F*, does not emit Alethe; cvc5 may prove less, which lowers the answer rate

findings.name: nanoda_lib (external Lean 4 checker)
findings.what: Independent Rust type checker for Lean 4 export files (lean4export), separate from Lean's kernel.
findings.steal: Re-check Lean certificates with nanoda in the replay script, the way Rocq has coqchk, so a Lean 'proved' is confirmed by a second kernel.
findings.moves: Independent replay of certificates
findings.evidence: Repo pushed 2026-09-22; checks lean4export output with configurable axiom handling
findings.risk: No performance numbers on the page; needs lean4export in the toolchain

findings.name: infini-gram
findings.what: Suffix-array engine that counts arbitrary-length n-grams and retrieves matching documents in trillion-token corpora in tens of milliseconds, with self-hostable indexes and a free API.
findings.steal: Add a heldout_audit pass that looks up long n-grams of each clean-182 problem and reference solution in public pretraining-corpus indexes. Self-index dawnr's own row store the same way for exact-overlap audits at any scale.
findings.moves: Contamination audits beyond dawnr's rows
findings.evidence: v2.6.0 released 2025-05-15, repo pushed 2026-01-24
findings.risk: Qwen's pretraining corpus is not public, so a hit is evidence and a miss is not proof; large indexes need disk

findings.name: Inspect (UK AISI eval framework)
findings.what: Open framework for LLM evaluations with tools, multi-turn dialogue and 200+ prebuilt evals, from the UK AI Security Institute.
findings.steal: Port score_levels and the panels to Inspect tasks so each published number comes with a standard log a third party can rerun. Use its scorer slot for the prover gate, not a model grader.
findings.moves: Reproducible evaluation that others recognise
findings.evidence: 7,902 commits, pushed 2026-10-05; over 200 prebuilt evaluations
findings.risk: Porting cost; the fetched page did not confirm llama.cpp support (use its OpenAI-compatible provider against dawnr's API)

findings.name: Data Provenance Collection
findings.what: Audit of 1,800+ fine-tuning datasets in 44 collections, with licence, creator and model-generated-source metadata, plus filter scripts.
findings.steal: Use its metadata and filters as an extra input to the --refuse-gpl and 'no GPT/Claude/Gemini/Llama-written rows' gate when admitting any outside dataset.
findings.moves: Data admission by graded trust without licence mistakes
findings.evidence: 44 collections, 1,800+ datasets; filters by licence and by model-generated provenance
findings.risk: Stale (last push 2025-03-26); not legal advice; covers older datasets only

findings.name: SAELens + nnsight (train your own SAE)
findings.licence: nnsight MIT; SAELens MIT (GitHub licence fields)
findings.what: nnsight reads and edits any PyTorch model's internals (also wraps vLLM); SAELens trains and loads sparse autoencoders.
findings.steal: Train a small SAE on Qwen3.5-4B residuals over dawnr's own prompts, since Qwen-Scope's weights are not permissively licensed. Use its features to explain refusals per domain (what kind of problem fails) and to find gaps in the panel.
findings.moves: Interpretability of a small open model, and understanding the answer-rate bottleneck
findings.evidence: nnsight v0.8.0.rc1 2026-09-09; SAELens pushed 2026-10-04
findings.risk: GPU time on the 4080; SAE features are descriptive, never a check

findings.licence: Qwen licence (model card: 'License: Qwen') — not permissive, idea only
findings.what: Qwen team's sparse-autoencoder suite: 14 groups across 7 Qwen3/Qwen3.5 backbones, e.g. 9B with 64K features, L0 50, on all 32 layers.
findings.steal: Copy the paper's uses (arXiv 2605.11887) with a self-trained SAE: steering against code-switching and repetition, and measuring benchmark redundancy and capability coverage of the clean-182.

findings.evidence: Released 2026-04-30; 9B checkpoint is 32 layer files, width 65,536, L0 50
findings.risk: Licence blocks shipping or training on the weights; no 4B checkpoint was seen on the pages fetched

findings.name: Large Language Monkeys (repeated sampling)
findings.licence: none stated on abs page (method only, nothing copied)
findings.what: Study showing coverage (any sample correct) grows log-linearly with sample count over four orders of magnitude.
findings.steal: Measure coverage@k (k=1..64) of the 4B on the clean 182 under the existing gate, then add a per-question sampling budget to bin/dawnr; the gate already picks the winner, so coverage becomes answer rate directly.
findings.moves: Answer rate (17/182) without new training
findings.evidence: DeepSeek-Coder-V2 on SWE-bench Lite: 15.9% at 1 sample to 56% at 250; with automatic verifiers coverage converts to accuracy, while majority vote and reward models plateau after a few hundred samples
findings.risk: CPU latency: k samples of a 4B is k times slower; needs a time budget and early stop on first proof

findings.name: TiCoder (test-driven user-intent formalization)
findings.licence: none stated on abs page (method only)
findings.what: Interactive loop where the system proposes tests and the user says yes or no, which both pins the intent and prunes candidate programs.
findings.steal: Before proving, show the person 1-3 concrete input/output examples drawn from disagreements among sampled candidates ('should f([3,1]) give [1,3]?'); approved examples are added to the t spec and filter candidates. A refusal from a weak spec turns into a question.
findings.moves: Spec bottleneck (right, complete specification) and use by non-programmers
findings.evidence: Average absolute +45.97% pass@1 within 5 user interactions across 4 LLMs and 2 datasets; earlier version 48.39% to 70.49% with one query on MBPP; user study n=15 showed better judgement of AI code and lower cognitive load
findings.risk: Numbers come from simulated users and large models; needs an offline-friendly UI in the page and CLI

findings.name: Amazon Bedrock Automated Reasoning checks
findings.what: Compiles a natural-language policy document into variables, typed rules and SMT, then checks each model answer against it.
findings.steal: Copy the shape for dawnr's documents mode: compile a person's rule document once into checked rules with IDs and saved test scenarios, and adopt the four verdicts (valid, invalid, satisfiable = true only under named assumptions, ambiguous = several readings) instead of answer-or-refuse.
findings.moves: Documents breadth and answer rate (conditional answers instead of refusals)
findings.evidence: Claims up to 99% accuracy detecting correct responses; policies up to 122,880 tokens (about 100 pages); rules carry IDs for traceability and SMT-LIB is viewable
findings.risk: Proprietary; the document-to-logic translation is itself LLM work and must be gated (round-trip or user-approved scenarios)

findings.name: Logic-LM
findings.what: LLM translates a word problem into FOL/CSP/SMT, a deterministic solver answers, solver errors drive self-refinement.
findings.steal: Take the translation prompts and solver glue as a new dawnr answer class 'rules and logic puzzles' checked by Z3, with the solver's model as the certificate; reuse its refinement-from-solver-error loop.
findings.moves: Breadth for ordinary people (scheduling, eligibility, logic questions) with a non-LLM check
findings.evidence: +39.2% over standard prompting and +18.4% over chain-of-thought across ProntoQA, ProofWriter, FOLIO, LogicalDeduction, AR-LSAT
findings.risk: Only 18 commits, looks unmaintained; bundled datasets carry their own licences (FOLIO etc. not checked here); translation faithfulness is not checked by the solver

findings.name: nl2postcond (Endres, Fakhoury, Chakraborty, Lahiri)
findings.licence: none stated on abs page (method only)
findings.what: Measures LLM-written postconditions by test-set correctness and by how many buggy variants they reject.
findings.steal: Add a spec-strength score to the gate and the data pipeline: a t spec must accept the reference and reject mutated implementations; rows whose spec kills few mutants are flagged as weak before training.
findings.moves: Spec completeness and data quality
findings.evidence: Generated postconditions caught 64 real historical Defects4J bugs (FSE 2024)
findings.risk: Mutant generation for t needs writing; mutants can be equivalent programs

findings.name: Conformal factuality (Mohri and Hashimoto)
findings.licence: none stated on abs page (method only)
findings.what: Back-off that removes sub-claims until the remaining output meets a calibrated correctness level.
findings.steal: Apply the back-off idea deterministically: when the full spec fails, release the strongest sub-specification that did prove ('proved: output sorted; not proved: same elements') and, for documents, the subset of sentences that quote-check.
findings.moves: Answer rate via honest partial answers
findings.evidence: 80-90% correctness guarantees while retaining the majority of the original output, on FActScore, NaturalQuestions and MATH
findings.risk: Their guarantee is statistical; dawnr must keep its parts exact and label partial answers clearly

findings.name: Grounded abstraction matching (CHI 2023) and ColDeco
findings.licence: none stated on abs page (idea only)
findings.what: Translates generated code back into a systematic, editable English utterance that re-invokes exactly that code; ColDeco adds helper columns and edge-case rows for checking table programs.
findings.steal: In the browser page, render each released t program and spec as a canonical English paraphrase generated by rule (not by the model), editable and re-runnable, plus intermediate-value columns for table questions.
findings.moves: Use by people who do not program; makes what was checked visible
findings.evidence: Think-aloud study n=24 improved users' grasp of the model's scope and of the phrasing it needs; ColDeco within-subjects study n=24, helper columns most valued (VL/HCC 2023)
findings.risk: Microsoft research prototypes; no code taken

findings.name: cedar-spec (verification-guided development)
findings.what: Lean formalization of the Cedar policy language plus differential randomized testing against the production Rust engine.
findings.steal: Write t's semantics once in Lean and differentially fuzz dawnr's t interpreter and its seven prover translations against it, so the trusted base (not just answers) has evidence.
findings.moves: Spaceship-grade trust in the checker itself
findings.evidence: 764 commits; components cedar-lean (proofs), cedar-drt (fuzzing/differential tests), cedar-policy-generators
findings.risk: Large upfront Lean work; needs a maintainer who knows Lean

findings.name: AlphaGeometry
findings.what: A 152M language model proposes only auxiliary constructions; a symbolic deduction engine (DD+AR) does the rest of the proof.
findings.steal: Shift the model's job toward the small creative piece (a loop invariant, a helper lemma, one spec clause) and let deterministic search and templates fill the remainder of the t program and proof.
findings.moves: Answer rate; small-model feasibility on CPU
findings.evidence: DDAR alone 14/30 IMO problems, with the 152M model 25/30; JGEX 198/231 to 228/231
findings.risk: Paper setup used 4 V100s and 250 CPU workers at beam 512; geometry is a narrow domain

findings.name: Pint
findings.what: Python library for quantities with units and dimensional analysis.
findings.steal: Run numeric answers with units through Pint in dawnr calc: refuse when dimensions disagree, convert exactly, and record units in the certificate.
findings.moves: Questions with numbers for ordinary people (recipes, travel, science homework)
findings.evidence: 3,008 commits; supports Python 3.12+; unit definitions from editable text files; NumPy/pandas integration
findings.risk: Float by default; must pair with dawnr's exact arithmetic (Fraction/Decimal magnitudes)

findings.name: docassemble
findings.what: Guided-interview engine (Python/YAML) that asks only the questions needed to reach a document or answer.
findings.steal: When a check fails for a missing fact, generate the specific follow-up question (docassemble's demand-driven question order) instead of a refusal.
findings.moves: Use by everyone; converts refusals into questions
findings.evidence: Licence page: MIT core; GPL tools (Pandoc, LaTeX) called only as subprocesses
findings.risk: Heavy server stack; take the pattern, not the platform

findings.name: Blawx
findings.what: Visual (Blockly) rules-as-code tool over s(CASP) that gives answers with logical explanations and hypothetical reasoning for non-programmers.
findings.steal: Borrow its explanation trees (each conclusion with the rule and fact that justify it) as the plain-language view of a dawnr certificate.
findings.moves: Explainable refusals and answers for non-programmers
findings.evidence: 1,134 commits; 198 open issues; self-described as not production-ready
findings.risk: Not production-ready; SWI-Prolog/s(CASP) dependency

findings.name: Equational Theories Project
findings.what: Tao's crowdsourced project settling about 22 million magma-law implications with ATPs and counterexample finders, every result certified in Lean.
findings.steal: Put cheap refuters (Mace4-style finite model search, random testing) in front of the seven provers to reject wrong specs fast, and mine automated-tool output as bulk training rows.
findings.moves: Data scarcity and prover time
findings.evidence: 4,694 laws, about 22M implications; tools used: Prover9, Mace4, Vampire, E, twee, Zipperposition, Z3, egg; 1,785 commits
findings.risk: Domain is abstract algebra, not programs; transfer is the pipeline, not the data

findings.name: VeriEQL
findings.licence: paper CC BY 4.0; artifact on Zenodo (licence not checked)
findings.what: SMT-based bounded equivalence checker for complex SQL that produces counterexamples.
findings.steal: For questions over a person's spreadsheets, answer with SQL run by an embedded engine and check candidate queries against each other; a counterexample table becomes the follow-up question.
findings.moves: Questions with numbers over tables
findings.evidence: Proves or disproves over 70% of 24,455 benchmarks; found bugs in MySQL and Apache Calcite (OOPSLA 2024)
findings.risk: Bounded equivalence only; equivalence between two model outputs is not correctness

findings.name: Query4Regex
findings.what: 1,000 regex-transformation tasks from natural language or a DSL, graded by DFA equivalence via pyformlang.
findings.steal: Add 'find text matching a pattern' as an answer class whose check is DFA equivalence or exhaustive matching on the person's text; use the set for evaluation.
findings.moves: Breadth with a decidable check
findings.evidence: Best five-shot: Phi-4-reasoning 14B 29.2%, gpt-oss-120B 28.3%, gemma-3-27B 20.2%
